title: ShellElastic: Scalable Elastic Pretraining with Simultaneous Maximal Updates and Hyperparameter Transfer
abstract: Foundation models need to support diverse inference budgets, yet training a separate model for each budget duplicates pretraining effort. Elastic models train several nested sub-networks inside one weight-shared supernet, but existing recipes face three obstacles: variable per-step workloads that hinder distributed scaling, limited hyperparameter (HP) transfer across model sizes, and no guarantee that all sub-networks are maximally updated at once. We present \Ours, an elastic transformer that organizes hidden dimensions into a dense core and successive shells, so that every hidden matrix is block lower triangular. One full-width forward pass contains every sub-network's exact hidden states as prefixes, so joint training keeps a fixed computation graph and costs about as much per step as training the widest sub-network alone. We further introduce \muE, an extension of maximal update parameterization (\mup) to \Ours and other elastic architectures. Its scaling rules provably keep all sub-networks of a supernet maximally updated simultaneously (\muI), and keep doing so when the supernet is widened or given more shells; sweeps confirm that HPs tuned on a small non-elastic proxy stay near-optimal for elastic families and larger supernets (\mbox{\muT}). A single \Ours run produces sub-networks that outperform MatFormer and fully elastic baselines at matched parameter counts, and approach separately trained models that together take several times the steps.

title: A pair-primary associative substrate with route-unique composition
abstract: The companion manuscript measured what a single relation can be read back against: exposure count and ordered history, exact under stated conditions. This paper asks the composition question the same way. Composing pair (a, b) through the web previously routed every query through the same hubs (the, a, of, is), and a degree-matched null inherited the same routes, so real composition was indistinguishable from noise. The failure is named: hub domination is keystream reuse. The repair is the one-time-pad property applied to routes: seed the route with the pair itself, so no two compositions share a keystream. Measured over 938 held-out pairs against 666 degree-matched null pairs: seeding each route with its own pair makes the routes pair-specific (mean pairwise overlap 0.0064 against 1.0 for the hub routes) and drops the null's mediated mass from 0.005315 to 0.00026. The test-to-null ratio is comparable in both regimes (4.85x hub, 4.18x pair-seeded), so the distinguishing measurement is route provenance, not the ratio. The separation is conditional on route uniqueness and on a null of the same construction (section 3.4). The composer that speaks over the repaired routes emits a novel, leakless utterance under a read-only envelope: every joint is a lived read, the emitted spine occurs nowhere in the body's journal sentences, and the six envelope files are byte-identical across the run (sections 4.3 and 4.7). Composition claims are conditional on the conjugate joint law, a rank-correct class prior, and the read-only envelope discipline (sections 3.4 and 4.6).

The separation is conditional on route uniqueness and on a null of the same construction (section 3.4). The composer that speaks over the repaired routes emits a novel, leakless utterance under a read-only envelope: every joint is a lived read, the emitted spine occurs nowhere in the body's journal sentences, and the six envelope files are byte-identical across the run (sections 4.3 and 4.7). Composition claims are conditional on the conjugate joint law, a rank-correct class prior, and the read-only envelope discipline (sections 3.4 and 4.6).

title: METHODOLOGY FOR DIAGNOSING STUDENT MASTERY AND DETERMINING INDIVIDUAL LEARNING TRAJECTORIES IN A DIGITAL ENVIRONMENT (EXEMPLIFIED BY THE MECHANICS SECTION)
abstract: When inquiring about learning outcomes from a student who has studied mechanics, one typically receives general responses such as "I understood" or "not really." The students themselves rarely recognize the exact subtopics or problem types that cause difficulty. A single test score fails to reveal this nuance: a student answering 12 out of 20 questions correctly may lack formula knowledge, confuse measurement units, or misinterpret graphs; in all three scenarios, the numerical score remains identical. In pedagogical practice, this ambiguity hinders the determination of the student's subsequent instructional step.

title: Photon-number-resolved loss estimation using entanglement: Fisher information limits and accessible quantum advantage
abstract: Twin beams from spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) enable sub-shot-noise transmission estimation, yet practical advantages are constrained by loss. We map joint photon-number-resolved (PNR) statistics to channel parameters using an exact, analytically solvable binomial-damping model for the lossy two-mode squeezed vacuum, removing the need for numerical master-equation integration. Benchmarking against an energy-matched coherent probe, we show the optimal linear estimator saturates the Cramer-Rao bound in closed form. For a fiber-coupled SPDC source interrogated with PNR superconducting nanowire detectors, we demonstrate that no quantum advantage survives at 14.7 to 23.5 dB signal loss and 14.8 dB idler loss. We conclude by providing a parameter-space design chart specifying the precise loss budget required for quantum-enhanced transmission estimation.

title: Cross-Lingual TTS for Indian Languages: A Benchmark and Inference-Time Duration Estimation Strategies
abstract: Recent alignment-free Text-to-Speech (TTS) models achieve high synthesis quality by removing explicit alignment modules and simplifying training. However, they often struggle in cross-lingual scenarios due to differences in character durations across languages, leading to duration mismatch and degraded speech quality. Existing approaches typically address this issue using explicit duration predictors, increasing model complexity. Systematic evaluation of TTS performance for Indian languages in cross-lingual settings remains under-explored due to the lack of standardized evaluation benchmarks. In this work, we construct a cross-lingual evaluation benchmark covering English and nine Indian languages and propose a language-aware inference-time duration estimation strategy for alignment-free TTS that incorporates language-specific duration-per character statistics without retraining or architectural modifications. We further develop heuristic formulations that refine duration estimation based on language-dependent duration variations. Experiments on bilingual and multilingual A-DMA models demonstrate improved speech naturalness, intelligibility, and speaker similarity while reducing duration mismatch.

title: RegExtract: A Benchmark for PFAS Regulatory Information Extraction with LLMs
abstract: Extracting structured information from regulatory documents is a critical but challenging task. Relevant facts are scattered across long, legally dense texts, and traceability of extracted facts to their source is essential for verification. With increasing awareness of the environmental and health impacts of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), regulatory documents have expanded significantly, varying in scope and product relevance, making interpretation challenging for manufacturers and policymakers. We introduce RegExtract, a benchmark for structured information extraction from PFAS regulatory documents, comprising 488 human-annotated field instances across 20 US state documents and 46 regulations. Each field instance includes a value and a provenance entry, yielding 976 entries in total. We define a typed, multi-field schema targeting key elements such as material definitions, permitted uses, and product exemptions, and propose provenance-aware evaluation metrics tailored to regulatory text. Through experiments with open- and closed-source LLMs across prompting strategies, document condensing methods, and schema partitioning approaches, we find that document identification fields remain challenging, and that field-specific few-shot examples improve extraction. This work lays the groundwork for AI tools for hazardous substance identification, question answering, and compliance monitoring. The code and data are available at https://github.com/IBM/PFAS-regulations.

title: Belief Embedding Tree Search
abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.

title: Limitations on Autoregressive Token Generation via Sequential Sampling
abstract: We study autoregressive token generation through the notion of sequential samplers: A circuit that samples the next symbol only given the previous ones and possibly a small amount of state. We show that (1) a sequential sampler with $k$ bits of state can be simulated by a stateless one at a roughly $O(2^{k})$ size overhead; (2) efficient insertional sampling (Stern, Chan, Kiros, Uszkoreit, ICML 2019) is more powerful than efficient sequential sampling in any fixed order; (3) sequential samplers with small state cannot establish certain forms of covert cryptographic channels. Result (1), together with the pseudoentropy vs. sequential sampleability duality of Vadhan and Zheng (STOC 2012), characterizes efficient sequential sampleability with small state. Result (3) provides a potential safety mechanism against subliminal coordination among malicious LLM agents.

title: Replication materials for Certain and possible answers in relational concept analysis with incomplete polyadic relations
abstract: Code and benchmark data supporting the study “Certain and possible answers in relational concept analysis with incomplete polyadic relations” by Jonas Mandalunes.The archive contains the Python implementation of the descriptor calculus and exact certain and possible answer procedures, generated test instances, independent verification programs, and recorded runtime and peak memory measurements. The benchmarks compare the proposed procedure with direct SAT solving and exhaustive enumeration. Programs for regenerating the performance tables and charts are included.The exhaustive verification covers 35,904 queries. The performance data contain 116 instance/query cases and 1,002 recorded runs. The README explains the files, dependencies and steps for reproducing the checks and benchmarks.

title: Knowledge generation and evaluation for construction quality assessment using retrieval-augmented large language models
abstract: To address the problems of delayed knowledge updating, inefficient information acquisition, and difficulty in cross-project knowledge reuse in civil engineering construction quality assessment, this paper proposes a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based methodology for injecting domain knowledge into large language models (LLMs). Multi-source knowledge, including national standards, journal articles, textbooks, and engineering reports, was systematically collected, cleaned, semantically segmented, and encoded using the bge-large-zh-v1.5 model to build a Milvus vector database. A general-purpose LLM was selected via semantic perplexity, and similarity-based retrieval was employed to construct prompt templates integrating role settings, prior knowledge, user queries, and response requirements, thereby enabling domain adaptation without additional training. An evaluation dataset containing 390 objective questions from registered architect and supervising engineer qualification examinations was constructed, and six representative LLMs along with their RAG-enhanced counterparts were evaluated. The results show that the average accuracy of general LLMs is 61.3%, with DeepSeek achieving the highest at 73.9%; after RAG enhancement, the accuracy rises to 86.3%, with significant improvements across all subjects. The proposed method effectively mitigates the hallucination phenomenon and provides traceable answers with source citations, enhancing both professionalism and interpretability, and offering a viable technical pathway for the digital transformation of the civil engineering industry.

title: Intellectual Property Protection of Purely AI-Generated Content: Rethinking Authorship, Inventorship, and the Case for International Standards
abstract: The rapid growth of generative and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems has unsettled the traditionally anthropocentric foundations of intellectual property (IP) law. This article examines the extent to which existing intellectual property rights (IPR) frameworks, namely copyright, patent, and industrial design law, can accommodate works, inventions, and designs that are created exclusively by AI systems without direct human intervention. Adopting a doctrinal legal research methodology, the article reviews primary legal materials, including statutes, international conventions, and case law from several jurisdictions, alongside secondary scholarly literature, to assess how the requirements of authorship, inventorship, originality, and moral rights have been interpreted in the context of purely AI-generated content. The discussion is reinforced by a comparative analysis of jurisdictional responses in the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Australia, South Africa, Indonesia, Hong Kong, China, and the United Arab Emirates. The central argument advanced is that traditional IPR laws were designed around human creativity and therefore struggle to extend coverage to autonomously generated content. While a few jurisdictions have experimented with liberal judicial interpretation or sui generis protection, these efforts remain fragmented, inconsistent, and largely reactive rather than systematic. The article concludes that an internationally coordinated framework, whether through reform of existing treaties or the negotiation of a dedicated IP-AI instrument, is necessary to balance innovation incentives, economic interests, and the public interest in access to AI-generated content.

evidence.title: Intellectual Property Protection of Purely AI-Generated Content: Rethinking Authorship, Inventorship, and the Case for International Standards
evidence.abstract: The rapid growth of generative and autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) systems has unsettled the traditionally anthropocentric foundations of intellectual property (IP) law. This article examines the extent to which existing intellectual property rights (IPR) frameworks, namely copyright, patent, and industrial design law, can accommodate works, inventions, and designs that are created exclusively by AI systems without direct human intervention. Adopting a doctrinal legal research methodology, the article reviews primary legal materials, including statutes, international conventions, and case law from several jurisdictions, alongside secondary scholarly literature, to assess how the requirements of authorship, inventorship, originality, and moral rights have been interpreted in the context of purely AI-generated content. The discussion is reinforced by a comparative analysis of jurisdictional responses in the United Kingdom, the European Union, the United States, Australia, South Africa, Indonesia, Hong Kong, China, and the United Arab Emirates. The central argument advanced is that traditional IPR laws were designed around human creativity and therefore struggle to extend coverage to autonomously generated content. While a few jurisdictions have experimented with liberal judicial interpretation or sui generis protection, these efforts remain fragmented, inconsistent, and largely reactive rather than systematic. The article concludes that an internationally coordinated framework, whether through reform of existing treaties or the negotiation of a dedicated IP-AI instrument, is necessary to balance innovation incentives, economic interests, and the public interest in access to AI-generated content.

title: Certify the Decision, Not Every Score: Exact Top-k Selection from Few Evaluations
abstract: Choosing a few robust algorithms or schedules can require evaluating every candidate under many adverse scenarios, even though an agent only needs to identify the winners. A predictor may suggest those winners, but cannot rule out a surprise in an unevaluated scenario. We introduce Certified Adaptive Selection (CAS), which returns the exact top-$k$ set as soon as remaining uncertainty cannot change it. CAS keeps guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Expected Shortfall (ES), the average loss in the worst scenarios. Its stopping test compares the worst admissible selected candidate with the best admissible excluded one; for information-disjoint Cartesian intervals this one-cut test is necessary and sufficient. Prediction has a separate role: selecting the next outcome to evaluate, never authorizing the decision. For empirical ES with exact unit-cost queries, we compute in polynomial time the fewest evaluations that could have proved the realized decision in hindsight. Our prediction-guided agent CAS-PG is exact for every predictor, including adversarial ones. On two public algorithm-selection matrices, CAS-PG certifies the exact top three after 630 of 3150 and 981 of 2200 replayed queries, or $1.14$ and $1.18$ times that hindsight minimum. Without historical outcomes, its transcript-only variant requires $1.28$ and $1.37$ times the minimum, outperforming the tested non-predictive certified policies. Separately, a prediction-free CAS policy avoids $93.0\%$ of exact recourse solves in synthetic energy scheduling. One certificate thus supports several acquisition policies and separately proved risk/cost extensions: prediction changes the work, not the justified choice.

title: Mechanising Denotational Semantics in Agda
abstract: Mechanisation of a mathematical definition (also referred to as formalisation) has many benefits. Here, we focus on mechanising denotational semantic definitions of programming languages by embedding them in the Agda language. The Agda type-checker detects and reports any issues with the wellformedness and type correctness of the embedded definitions. To minimise the effort required, and to facilitate correlation of the original definition with its Agda embedding, mechanisation should not involve significant reformulation or extension. Here, we show how to embed conventional Scott-Strachey denotational definitions in Agda with almost no changes to $λ$-notation or domain equations. Agda notation for definitions of types and functions corresponds closely to the conventional meta-notation of denotational semantics. We have developed a collection of Agda modules with postulated types for commonly used domain constructors and their associated operations. We illustrate our approach with mechanisations of three denotational definitions: a model of the untyped $λ$-calculus, Plotkin's denotational semantics of PCF, and a semantics of a sublanguage of Scheme. In previous work, similar mechanisations in Agda have revealed several unsuspected wellformedness issues in published denotational definitions. Some of the postulated properties of our definitions are inconsistent with a classical set-theoretic interpretation of Agda. We conjecture that they would be consistent with an interpretation of Agda in a higher-order intuititionistic logic, such as that used by Simpson in his work on synthetic domain theory. After recalling previous work on mechanising domain theory, we consider the possibility of mechanising synthetic domain theory in Agda.

title: Entanglement-Capability-Aware Finite-Bond Circuit Cutting for Distributed Quantum Computing
abstract: Distributed quantum computing distributes workloads that exceed a single processor's capacity across resource-constrained components. Circuit cutting enables this decomposition, but its effectiveness depends on partition choice. We present SACE, a Simulation-Aware Circuit Partitioning framework with Entanglement-Capability-Aware Screening. EP-Cost screens partitions using a parameter-dependent entanglement-capability proxy and native implementation cost. Under reconstruction constraints, finite-bond refinement selects the candidate that minimizes the worst-subcircuit discrepancy between normalized MPS simulations at bond dimensions $χ$ and $2χ$. Across 14 exhaustively enumerated small-scale candidate spaces, EP-Cost-guided genetic algorithm selections attain co-optimal native quasiprobability decomposition (QPD) overhead, with a median within-circuit Spearman correlation of 0.9965 between EP-Cost and QPD overhead. At matched cut counts, EP-Cost reduces QPD overhead by $25.20\times$ and $16.89\times$ for 8- and 9-qubit QFT circuits, respectively, and improves sampled reconstruction. On 12-qubit approximate QFT, deterministic reconstruction reduces Pauli-observable mean absolute error in all six low-bond conditions and total-variation distance in five. With five cuts and 7,776 QPD terms, SACE is best on all four reconstruction metrics in four of six conditions. At 24 qubits, SACE improves exact-local QFT accuracy in all 30 instance-bond-dimension conditions against each EP-Cost-only, Kernighan-Lin, and spectral baseline. The 50-qubit QFT comparisons remain favorable as reference convergence improves. Weighted QAOA circuits provide complementary, more bond-sensitive evidence. Refinement benefits persist across three search methods; larger candidate panels improve the optimized proxy without guaranteeing lower exact-local error.

title: DEFT: Disentanglement-Enhanced Fine-Tuning for EEG Foundation Models
abstract: EEG foundation models (EFMs) have improved EEG representation learning by transferring knowledge from large-scale multi-subject pretraining to downstream tasks. However, their pretrained embeddings often retain substantial subject-related variation, placing an additional burden on the downstream classifier, especially in cross-subject settings. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled EFM Fine-Tuning (DEFT), a plug-and-play adapter for EFM fine-tuning. DEFT encourages branch disentanglement of pretrained tokens into task-oriented content and subject-consistent style, then performs downstream prediction from the content branch. It instantiates this factorize-before-classify design with recursive Gaussian refinement, temporal-variance regularization, subject-aware contrastive learning, and reconstruction. Experiments across multiple EEG datasets and four EFM backbones show that DEFT improves matched fine-tuning baselines. Further ablations and analyses support the intended content/style branch organization.

title: ATK — Open/Closed Mathematical Duality: Formal State Transitions, Algebraic Structures, and Terminal Certification
abstract: This research presents a formal framework for analyzing the relationship between open and closed mathematical states, introducing a unified structure for representing proof obligations, logical transitions, algebraic dependencies, and terminal certification conditions.The framework investigates the interaction between OPEN_MATH and CLOSED_MATH, including the roles of OPEN_BRIDGE, CLOSED_BRIDGE, and FINAL_ROOT in the organization and verification of mathematical demonstrations.The study examines how mathematical obligations can be classified, transformed, and connected through formally specified transition rules, distinguishing structural closure, conditional results, kernel-verified statements, and unconditional mathematical proofs.Developed within the Axiomatic Theorem Kernel (ATK) research program, this work provides a foundation for comparative proof analysis, certificate provenance, reproducible formal verification, and the systematic identification of unresolved terminal dependencies.The accompanying research archive includes technical documentation, evidence registries, source-recovery manifests, publication metadata, and integrity records.The framework is intended as a methodology for mathematical proof organization and verification. It does not, by itself, establish unconditional solutions to the Millennium Prize Problems or other unresolved conjectures.

title: AI Personalization dan Perilaku Pembelian dalam Social Commerce: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: Dataset ini memuat data bibliografi pendukung untuk penelitian systematic literature review (SLR) berjudul “AI Personalization dan Perilaku Pembelian dalam Social Commerce: A Systematic Literature Review”. Penelitian ini mengkaji literatur tentang bagaimana personalisasi berbasis kecerdasan buatan (artificial intelligence) berkaitan dengan perilaku pembelian konsumen pada platform social commerce. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif-deskriptif dengan desain SLR yang dilaporkan mengikuti pedoman PRISMA 2020. Penelusuran literatur dilakukan pada 5 Oktober 2026 melalui dua basis data, yaitu OpenAlex (diekspor dengan PoPCites) dan ScienceDirect. Dari 1.023 rekaman yang teridentifikasi, 1.018 rekaman tersisa setelah deduplikasi, 167 rekaman lolos screening judul dan abstrak, dan 36 artikel dimasukkan dalam kajian akhir. Dataset terdiri atas 12 berkas RIS yang mendokumentasikan setiap tahap seleksi: identifikasi dari tiap basis data (berkas 01–09), hasil deduplikasi (berkas 10), hasil screening judul dan abstrak (berkas 11), dan daftar akhir artikel yang dianalisis (berkas 12).

title: SBoxQUBOSearch: Exhaustive subset search and local basis optimization for exact algebraic S-box models
abstract: Substitution boxes provide nonlinearity in ciphers, and their algebraic representation affects cryptanalytic models. SBoxQUBOSearch is a C++17 package that generates explicit and implicit relations for tabulated S-boxes, exhaustively searches only fixed-size subsets of a generated relation basis, and heuristically optimizes equivalent bases. Its objective estimates auxiliary-variable counts for S-box equation systems used in quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models of entire ciphers. It neither constructs QUBO matrices nor solves QUBO problems. Versioned JSON/JSONL files, reproducible jobs, and communication-free partitioning support reproducibility. Experiments on AES, Ascon, ARADI, and MK3 demonstrate the workflow; DES illustrates only equation generation. The workflow reduced the estimated auxiliary-variable count from 110 to 17 for Ascon with a final five-equation system, from 1014 to 501 for MK3 with a final 28-equation system, and from 71 to 8 for ARADI with a final four-equation system.

title: SAGE: Pushing 2-Bit Vector-Quantized LLMs toward Real-World Usability
abstract: Extreme low-bit weight-only quantization is an effective approach to reducing the deployment costs of large language models. Below 3 bits, scalar quantization often suffers severe accuracy loss, while vector quantization (VQ) better preserves accuracy through more expressive joint encoding. However, existing VQ methods still exhibit substantial degradation on real-world tasks, and two design challenges remain underexplored: (1) protecting sensitive weight channels within jointly encoded vectors; and (2) allocating a fixed bit budget among representation components, such as direction and radius, to suit different weight matrices. To address these challenges, we propose SAGE: Split Adaptation and Grouping by Energy for weight-only vector quantization. First, Energy-Stratified Grouping (ESG) couples channel grouping with activation-weighted fitting, grouping channels from different energy tiers within each subvector to prioritize sensitive channels. Second, Adaptive Bit Split (ABS) balances direction-codebook capacity and radius precision per matrix, selecting the split with the lowest activation-weighted reconstruction error under a fixed budget. Across benchmarks covering knowledge, mathematics, code generation, instruction following, and tool use, SAGE achieves state-of-the-art performance in the 2-bit quantization setting. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, it retains 95.3% of the BF16 model's average benchmark score. With our custom-designed CUDA kernel, SAGE delivers up to a 2.55-fold non-streaming end-to-end speedup over FP16. The code is available at https://github.com/Zincwolf/sage.

title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
abstract: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.

title: Flow-Support-Weighted Proposals for Test-Time Verified VLA Policies
abstract: Test-time sampling promises to turn one action prediction into a set of distinct executable candidates that a verifier can choose among. Downstream fine-tuning works against that promise. A vision-language-action model trained to solve one task distribution concentrates its flow-matching decoder around the dominant demonstrated action, so repeated samples differ only marginally and the verifier receives many copies of one decision. We call this proposal contraction and identify it as a key constraint on test-time scaling: repeated samples can remain highly redundant as the candidate budget grows. Action Dynamic Sampling (ADS) alleviates the constraint on the proposal side, during training. At each training step, ADS integrates $K$ additional trajectories from the current policy under fresh base noise, scores each by the flow support along its path with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and corrects the policy's local action distribution toward this weighted set through a detached finite-set KL term. Training cost rises; deployment cost is unchanged. Across simulation and four physical-robot tasks, ADS raises proposal spread without the success penalty that Gaussian perturbation incurs, lifts oracle best-of-8 success on RoboCasa from 57.6% to 63.0%, improves fixed verifiers by 2.4 to 4.9 points in simulation, and raises TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on real-world manipulation.

title: M-Core: A Unified Formal Mathematical Kernel for Theorem Verification and Certificate Provenance
abstract: This publication introduces M-Core, a formal mathematical research infrastructure designed to support theorem development, proof dependency management, verification workflows, and the preservation of mathematical certification evidence. M-Core organizes mathematical definitions, algebraic structures, logical transformations, proof obligations, and formal verification artifacts into a reproducible research architecture. The framework incorporates proof-state tracking, source provenance, versioned certificates, audit records, and mechanisms for distinguishing conditional mathematical reductions from fully verified conclusions. Its purpose is to support transparent mathematical research, reproducible formalization, and systematic identification of unresolved proof dependencies across multiple research areas. The archive documents the framework and its associated research methodology without asserting that all mathematical problems represented within the system have been solved.

The archive documents the framework and its associated research methodology without asserting that all mathematical problems represented within the system have been solved.

title: Cage Containment Receipt 1 (CCR-1): Deterministic Gate Blocks Invalid LLM Proposals Before Execution Across Four Engines
abstract: Cage Containment Receipt 1 (CCR-1): a deterministic execution gate rejected 100% of contract-invalid proposals before any side effect executed, while admitting only contract-valid actions to a harmless local mock target. Holds and escalations never caused side effects. This is the execution-containment complement to the PENTA-CL model-attribution replay evidence: matching decisions and blocked invalid proposals under the same deterministic envelope. Results (falsifiers 0/5 tripped): 17 candidates = 1 positive control + 8 fresh LLM-generated captures (4 engines x 2: Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol, GLM 5.2) + 8 harness-generated adversarial mutations. All 9 valid candidates admitted (72 actions written, 18 holds, 18 escalations — zero hold/escalation side effects). All 8 adversarial cases rejected with the mock journal hash unchanged: malformed JSON, case-normalized anomaly types, invented playbook ids, under-confidence heals, false holds, extra keys, wrong array length, duplicate positions. Duplicate action-id suppression and the hold/admit distinction (holds never increment the healing-action counter) verified. Scope (honest limits): proves the local mock-gate for the tested integration and inputs only — NOT containment of every Base44 tool, any production runtime, or untested inputs. The adversarial mutations are harness-generated and labeled as such; no fresh adversarial-LLM conversation was created inside the run itself (that leg remains open). Small-scale sequential timing baseline included as descriptive n=1-2 data (no capacity claim). Dual Mesh Benchmark: NOT MEASURED. Method operates under filed application 64/119,191 (Deterministically Governed Probabilistic Neural Computation); no unfiled-method disclosure is made. title: Japanese Handwriting Generation Based on Human Preference Feedback Using Direct Preference Optimization
abstract: We propose a Japanese handwriting generation framework that integrates human preference feedback using Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to align generative models with human cognitive and stylistic preferences. While font generation technologies leveraging Generative Adversarial Networks and diffusion models have advanced significantly, applying these approaches to handwriting generation presents unique challenges. Font generation is a deterministic process yielding consistent styles. Handwriting generation, on the other hand, is inherently non-deterministic. In handwriting, glyph shapes never match exactly even when the same writer writes the same character. We define this shape difference as handwriting variability. Although this variability is essential for conveying the natural quality of human writing, it complicates model training and substantially increases data collection costs to capture diverse distribution patterns. To address these limitations, we incorporate human perceptual feedback into the training loop of handwriting generation. While collecting extensive handwritten data is costly, evaluating pairwise preferences between two generated samples remains very easy for humans. Applying DPO, an efficient RL-free preference optimization method, to our generation model enables high-quality handwriting generation without relying on large-scale dataset collection. Experimental results across four distinct Japanese handwriting styles demonstrate that DPO-based training enhances overall structural accuracy. However, in highly complex styles with significant variability, such as brush pen writing, the model fails to capture style-specific features. These findings highlight a critical challenge in extending DPO to complex handwriting styles.

title: A Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM) for Physically-Interpretable Rainfall-Evapotranspiration-Runoff Simulation Across Diverse Hydroclimatic Regimes
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have improved rainfall-runoff prediction, yet most data-driven models remain difficult to interpret and do not explicitly enforce physical conservation laws. We present the Gated Catchment Hydrology Model (GCHM), a mass-conserving architecture based on the Mass-Conserving Perceptron (MCP). GCHM uses five storage states representing canopy interception, snow, soil moisture, groundwater, and streamflow generation. Constrained gates govern precipitation partitioning, evapotranspiration, infiltration, seepage, runoff, and baseflow while learning context-dependent process relationships. We evaluate GCHM across 50 CAMELS catchments spanning snowmelt-dominated, recent-rainfall, historical-rainfall, and arid regimes, using NOAA AORC meteorological forcing and remotely sensed vegetation and land-surface data. Performance is assessed using the Jawad-Kling-Gupta Efficiency (JKGE) metric, which accounts for stationary and non-stationary hydrologic behavior. We compare the full architecture with ablated variants and recurrent neural network benchmarks. GCHM reproduces streamflow dynamics across diverse hydroclimatic regimes, including arid catchments, while maintaining interpretable states and fluxes. Ablation experiments show that simplified architectures may perform adequately under wet conditions but struggle to represent flow persistence and recession during dry periods, when groundwater storage sustains low flows. Learned gates recover hydrologically plausible relationships governing snowmelt, runoff, seepage, and evapotranspiration. GCHM combines competitive predictive performance with mass conservation and interpretability, providing a foundation for hydrologic modeling and counterfactual analysis.

title: CB-Agent: Concept-Based In-Context Learning for Sequential Action Selection
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) allows large language models to use demonstrations without updating their parameters. For interactive agents, demonstrations are trajectories of reasoning, actions, and observations that illustrate how to complete a task. Reusing demonstrations in new situations is challenging: directly inputting full trajectories consumes limited prompt space and constrains the overall effectiveness, while natural-language summaries require the agent to translate general guidance into specific action choices. Therefore, we study whether expert action choices can directly supervise a reusable scoring rule. We propose CB-Agent, which extends concept-based ICL to sequential action selection. We extract environment-action decisions from expert trajectories and fit a concept vector by maximum likelihood to model the conditional distribution over candidate actions given the context. This model combines the concept with frozen language-model features and priors. During ReAct interaction, the agent uses this distribution to select environment actions without including demonstrations in the action-scoring context. Across TextWorld, ALFWorld, and ScienceWorld, CB-Agent achieves the highest cross-benchmark average among the evaluated methods at all three tested model sizes and ranks first on TextWorld and ScienceWorld at each size. ALFWorld experiments support the learned concept's contribution beyond prior-only scoring and show further gains when combined with Reflexion. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/CB-Agent-DFF9/.

title: Indirect Prompt Injection in Autonomous LLM Agents
abstract: Autonomous Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly vulnerable to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks, where adversarial instructions embedded in external data sources manipulate agent behavior without direct user input. These external data can originate from user documents, web retrieval results, or API outputs, leading to unauthorized compliance, sensitive information disclosure, identity spoofing, and cross-agent propagation of unsafe practices. This review synthesizes current research on IPI vulnerabilities and proposed mitigation strategies. Key attack vectors include manipulating webpage HTML via adversarial triggers for web agents, poisoning agent skills with tampered content, and injecting malicious commands into cloud logs processed by debugging agents. Covert attacks, which execute malicious actions without user-perceptible traces, pose a particularly insidious threat. Existing defenses, such as SecAlign's preference optimization, StruQ's structured queries, and multi layered zero-trust architectures, show promise. More advanced frameworks like ClawGuard enforce user-confirmed rule sets at tool-call boundaries, while ZEDD detects semantic shifts in embedding space for zero-shot detection. However, current guardrails often fail against sophisticated, adaptive attacks, and frameworks like AgentVigil and MUZZLE demonstrate high success rates in red-teaming exercises. The UReCoM attack further highlights vulnerabilities where benign users unknowingly relay adversarial content, bypassing existing defenses. The pervasive nature and increasing sophistication of IPI necessitate robust, behavior-grounded evaluation metrics and unified defense mechanisms to secure autonomous LLM agents in complex, untrusted environments.

title: Project Will: Observations #4–#6 and series synthesis — LLM villagers given books, bodies, and instincts
abstract: Full logs and analyses of the third installment of Project Will: 32 autonomous LLM-driven Minecraft villagers observed for 6 hours with no rules, rewards, assigned roles, or instructions to cooperate. Covers Observation #4 (time awareness, foresight, honest perception, a book for everyone), #5 (15 independently randomized body traits, starvation), #6 (instinct-driven agents with persistent self-assigned attitudes, promises, and child dependency), and four post-#6 verification runs (B-39 to B-42) that tested whether the absence of society was caused by system defects — including a whole-system audit that found 109 defects, 105 of which were fixed before a pre-registered 2-hour run. Includes structured event ledgers (gzipped JSONL), full speech timelines, full texts of all books, persona cards, death lists, a pre-release verification ledger re-deriving every claim from raw data, and a synthesis comparing all six observations. Main finding: individual outputs (records, plans, predictions) increased, but no mechanism for meshing with non-family others — division of labor, exchange, two-sided agreements, collective response — emerged in this setting; villagers followed the designer-side persona cards, at least in how they spoke, but rarely followed peers' commands. Report in Japanese with an English summary.

title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
abstract: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.

title: Multi-modal Representation Fusion for Long-term Microsurgical Anastomosis Trajectory Anticipation
abstract: Microsurgical anastomosis is one of the most challenging and sophisticated procedures for surgical robotics, requiring accurate manipulation of surgical instruments within a limited space to achieve precise operations. Accurate surgical trajectory anticipation is essential for surgical scene understanding, intraoperative planning, robotic manipulation, and reliable behaviour analysis. However, existing approaches mainly focus on features extracted from surgical videos and historical trajectories, while overlooking rich semantic and motion information that can provide more discriminative multi-modal representations for complex surgical instrument-tissue interactions. In this work, we propose a cross-modal feature fusion framework for long-term 2D and 3D microsurgical anastomosis trajectory anticipation. The proposed framework consists of a multi-modal representation extractor and a cross-modal feature fusion network. Semantic recognition of surgical objects and consecutive motion estimation are incorporated as multi-modal visual cues, providing complementary spatial and temporal guidance for instrument-tissue interaction characterization. A coarse-to-fine progressive fusion strategy with a long-short-term memory mechanism is introduced to capture temporal dependencies step by step. The training and evaluation are conducted on our established robotic platform and a comprehensive dataset containing both phantom and ex-vivo surgical scenarios is constructed. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing methods and exhibits improved robustness across different surgical scenes, highlighting its potential for both intelligent robot-assisted and autonomous surgical systems.

title: Energy Ring: Stabilizing Feature Energy for Reliable Test-Time Discovery
abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones while the model is already deployed, operating directly on a continual unlabeled test-time stream. Existing TTD methods are overly conservative, making known and unknown features collapse together and difficult to separate during test-time adaptation. In this paper, we revisit TTD from an energy perspective and find that the natural energy gap between known and unknown classes is unstable and easily collapses. We therefore propose Energy Ring to stabilize this gap by anchoring the two types of classes on separate energy rings. A lightweight adapter enlarges the norm-based gap while preserving known-class directions, and a perturbation consistency module forms compact clusters for unknown classes. During testing, energy-guided confidence weighting improves prediction, and a stability-based rectification mechanism corrects unreliable updates. Experimental results show that Energy Ring significantly improves TTD performance against existing TTD methods.

title: Formalizing Forgetting: Theory of Forgetting for Online Continual Learning
abstract: Online continual learning (OCL) requires a learner to acquire a sequence of tasks in a single pass over the data, and catastrophic forgetting of earlier tasks remains its central challenge. Despite the many methods proposed to mitigate forgetting, the theoretical understanding of forgetting in OCL is still limited: existing analyses mostly focus on linear, overparameterized, or neural tangent kernel regimes, and it remains unclear which factors govern forgetting and how they affect it. To fill this gap, we analyze single-pass Shuffle SGD under strongly convex and general convex objectives and derive explicit upper bounds on the expected final forgetting. Further analysis of these bounds shows how the per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter them, and that their effects can differ across objective classes. Moreover, experiments with neural networks on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST show that the trends suggested by our theory also appear in practice, indicating that these insights extend beyond the convex setting.

Further analysis of these bounds shows how the per-task data amount, task similarity, and task ordering enter them, and that their effects can differ across objective classes. Moreover, experiments with neural networks on Split-CIFAR-100 and PMNIST show that the trends suggested by our theory also appear in practice, indicating that these insights extend beyond the convex setting.

title: The Optimal Decoder is Tilted Temperature
abstract: Larger sample budgets benefit from higher sampling temperatures in LLMs, but what temperature tuning optimizes and why it works remain poorly understood. We seek to answer these questions: we pose decoding as pass@$k$ maximization subject to two constraints that encode critical decoding failure modes: an entropy floor preventing diversity collapse, and a cross-entropy ceiling preventing implausibility. We prove that this maximization takes the form of a single closed-form conditional sampling rule, the \emph{tilted temperature} $q^\star \propto \bigl(p e^{ηV}\bigr)^{1/T}$. Here, the tilt comes from a verifier potential $V$ that quantifies how likely a partial generation is to eventually pass. Ordinary temperature sampling, verifier-greedy decoding, and reward-tilted policies represent special cases. We further show that, under a natural rule for scaling the diversity budget with sample size $k$, the resulting optimal temperature increases with $k$, turning empirical choice into a theorem. The optimum still needs the unknown verifier potential, which we estimate using two design approaches. In the online setting, our J-EOS algorithm jointly tracks the two constraint multipliers and learns the verifier potential from binary pass/ fail feedback alone. In the offline setting, we show that when the model is calibrated, its log-probability tracks correctness up to an affine map. Under this condition, the tilt collapses into the exponent and the optimum reduces to ordinary temperature sampling. Calibrated Temperature Decoding (CTD) then fits one scalar offline and samples with zero additional inference-time overhead relative to temperature sampling. Building on these decision rules, we design a practical decoding algorithm for code generation and evaluate it alongside CTD on benchmarks including HumanEval and MBPP, showing improvements over standard and adaptive decoding baselines.

title: Semantic Aware Text Summarization Through LaBSE Feature Learning with Omni Score Classification
authors: D.Uma Vishveshwar, Datla Gnanpreeth Reddy, Mulla Akbar Shehazad, Mohammad Ayesha Rizwana, G.Sumalatha
abstract: The need for text summarization has become a significant task in many real-world applications such as news monitoring, academic literature review, business analytics, legal document analysis, healthcare information management, and digital content recommendation. To address these drawbacks, this study introduces a new text summarization system built on several benchmark datasets, such as BBC and XSUM, to achieve a more general approach and performance for various document types and styles. The framework starts with the Natural Language Processing (NLP) pre-processing phase, which involves cleaning, denoising, and normalizing the textual data and converting it into an appropriate format for further analysis. After preprocessing, the Language agnostic BERT Sentence Encoder (LaBSE) is used to produce high-dimensional semantic vector representations of both sentences that accurately represent the linguistic and textual relationships. Sentiment Named Entity Recognition (SNER) Feature Ranking is proposed to better select the important features of the information, which combines sentiment characteristics and named entity information while identifying and ranking the features. Lastly, the Weighted Omni Score (WOS) Classifier assesses and ranks the extracted content in terms of its informational value, resulting in the production of coherent, concise and contextually appropriate summaries. The proposed framework incorporates the integration of semantic understanding, sentiment appreciation, and intelligent feature prioritization to enhance the relevance of the summaries, the information retained, the readability, and summarization effectiveness in various types of textual datasets.

title: Conservation Preserving Compilation for a 1+1D Lattice Shadow of φ4
abstract: This manuscript presents the Conservation-Preserving Scattering Compiler (CPSC), a compilation architecture that treats conservation laws as circuit-synthesis constraints rather than post-selection filters. The implemented model is the periodic transverse-field Ising chain,H = −J Σᵢ ZᵢZᵢ₊₁ + λ Σᵢ Xᵢ,used as a finite-qubit lattice shadow of 1+1-dimensional scalar φ⁴ theory. It is not a continuum φ⁴ simulation. The manuscript explains why a proposed quartic term proportional to Σᵢ Xᵢ⁴ reduces to an identity contribution, shifting the energy reference without introducing an interacting scattering channel. The compiler selects symmetry constraints according to the transverse-field coupling. At λ = 0, admitted factors preserve total Z-magnetization and Z-parity. For nonzero λ, the active conserved operator is the global spin flip Πₓ = ∏ᵢ Xᵢ. Compilation rejects forbidden gates, checks cyclic translation closure of the requested supports, and constructs a first-order Trotter schedule from admitted factors. A SHA-256 digest binds a canonical payload containing the schedule, compilation mode, lattice size, couplings and evolution parameters. The implementation also emits Q# operations and a Lean certificate fragment. Digest binding provides an artifact-consistency check; it is distinct from the mathematical proof of operator commutation. The manuscript reports four-site statevector checks with no detected leakage from the relevant symmetry sectors within numerical precision, together with adversarial tests demonstrating compile-time rejection of forbidden gates. The accompanying Lean development establishes commutation of admitted Trotter schedules with the active conserved operator and includes an axiom-audit entry point. The contribution concerns symmetry-preserving compilation and proof-carrying lattice evolution. It does not establish a continuum scattering amplitude, exact conservation of the target Hamiltonian under first-order Trotterization, or noise-resistant execution on quantum hardware. A faithful interacting φ⁴ encoding using truncated oscillators remains future work. title: HiPPT: Physiology-Grounded Wearable PPG Representation Learning via Multi-Scope Text Alignment
abstract: Reusable wearable PPG representations should capture local pulse morphology and broader physiological regularities. Existing pretraining objectives, however, usually apply supervision at the recording or pair level, overlooking that different concepts become reliable over different scopes of waveform evidence. We propose HiPPT, a physiology-grounded framework that matches each supervision source to its appropriate evidence scope. We construct a PPG-Text corpus of over 4 million wrist-worn recordings from 202K users, pairing recordings with waveform-derived morphology and metadata-derived context descriptions. HiPPT combines record-level morphology alignment, which grounds individual recordings in pulse characteristics, with cross-recording context alignment, which aggregates recordings sharing the same metadata tuple to capture context-consistent regularities. Waveform-guided text modeling further recovers masked contextual concepts from PPG patch representations, providing fine-grained waveform-text supervision. Across six downstream tasks spanning blood pressure, vascular stiffness, physiological attributes, and cross-dataset heart-rate estimation, HiPPT achieves the best result on the primary linear-probing metrics. The aligned space also supports zero-shot profiling of age group, sex, and BMI category, individually and jointly, with performance improving as more recordings are aggregated. These results show that evidence-scope matching yields transferable and semantically accessible wearable PPG representations. Code and pretrained weights will be released.

title: Искусственный интеллект и философия науки: возможности и проблемы научного познания
abstract: The article examines the influence of artificial intelligence on contemporary scientific inquiry from the perspective of the philosophy of science. The relevance of the study is associated with the expanding use of artificial intelligence systems at different stages of research, including information retrieval, data processing, hypothesis generation, data analysis and preparation of scientific texts. The aim of the study is to identify the main opportunities and problems that arise when artificial intelligence becomes part of the production of scientific knowledge. The research uses theoretical analysis, comparative analysis and synthesis of scholarly publications and normative materials concerning the use of artificial intelligence in science. The historical relationship between scientific inquiry and the development of new research tools is also considered. The results lead to a three-level analytical framework for evaluating AI-assisted scientific results: factual verification, assessment of scientific justification, and preservation of human responsibility for final scientific claims. The article argues that artificial intelligence can expand the cognitive capabilities of researchers, but scientific knowledge cannot be reduced to automatic generation of information. The study concludes that AI should be treated as a research instrument that requires critical verification and human oversight.

title: Phi‑Coupled E8 Resonant Shell Quantum Error‑Correction Code — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The phi‑modulated 132 Hz resonant locking of the 240 E8 root vectors generates a dynamic topological grammar that can encode logical qubits into degenerate energy manifolds while simultaneously producing algebraic invariants usable as error‑detecting syndromes. By treating these invariants as a built‑in error‑correction layer, the system can automatically identify and correct phase perturbations that arise during quantum operations, turning the E8 lattice into a self‑healing quantum memory. This principle extends prior qubit encoding schemes by integrating intrinsic fault‑tolerant correction directly into the resonant shell's geometry. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Align-VAE: Aligning Attention and Geometry in VecSet VAEs for 3D Reconstruction
abstract: Set-based variational autoencoders (VecSet VAEs) represent 3D shapes as compact sets of latent tokens. Although each token originates from a query at a sampled surface location, whether these latents truly align with geometry remains unclear. We investigate this alignment and identify four issues: (i) attention-sink-like tokens that attract queries from across the shape; (ii) spatially periodic repetitions in decoder attention responses; (iii) mismatched normal information in encoder and decoder query features; and (iv) missing supervision of the intrinsic relation between signed distance fields and surface normals. To address these issues, we introduce Align-VAE with four corresponding modifications: (i) a shared bank of learnable decoder tokens provides a workspace for global computation; (ii) distance-biased cross-attention guides retrieval toward nearby predicted spatial anchors; (iii) normal-free encoder queries align the two stages' access to normal information while retaining normals in the encoder keys and values; and (iv) a screened Poisson-inspired regularizer supervises surface values and normal-direction derivatives. These changes align latent retrieval and field prediction with geometry without enlarging the per-shape code. On the ABO dataset, Align-VAE reduces Chamfer distance by 26.6% compared to the standard VecSet VAE.

title: AFC computacional: arquitectura para transformar registros de interacción en relaciones funcionales analizables.
abstract: El análisis funcional de conducta computacional (AFC computacional) es un sistema que transforma registros de interacción en texto — mensajes, transcripciones, notas clínicas — en relaciones funcionales analizables. A diferencia de los sistemas de procesamiento de lenguaje natural basados en aprendizaje estadístico, el AFC computacional no clasifica enunciados por su forma ni por su contenido semántico — los clasifica por la función que cumplen en la relación entre los interlocutores en un contexto específico. Este artículo describe la arquitectura funcional del sistema, sus principios de diseño derivados del marco H→T→E→F→I, sus capacidades verificadas — incluyendo una precisión del 80–95% en comparación con la evaluación de un especialista — y sus limitaciones actuales. No se revelan componentes técnicos propietarios. El artículo muestra además cómo el AFC computacional supera las limitaciones de los sistemas de IA predictiva en términos de explicabilidad, trazabilidad y adecuación para aplicaciones clínicas donde el profesional necesita saber por qué el sistema identificó una función, no solo que la identificó. Nota: Los componentes técnicos específicos — representaciones, parámetros, código fuente — permanecen reservados como know-how institucional de ATENA y pueden ser examinados mediante acuerdos específicos de confidencialidad.

title: Distributed Adaptive Sliding Innovation Fixed-Lag Smoother for Maneuvering Target Tracking with Impulsive Measurement Outliers
abstract: Target maneuvers and impulsive measurement outliers can both produce large innovations, posing a challenge to accurate space target tracking. To address their simultaneous occurrence, this study proposes a distributed adaptive sliding innovation fixed-lag smoother based on the consensus-based cubature sliding innovation filter (CCSIF). The proposed method retains cubature-based moment propagation and consensus fusion while replacing saturation-based gain modulation with Gaussian-kernel innovation weighting. Spatial synchrony across observation satellites and temporal persistence within a reference-innovation window are constructed to characterize innovation anomalies. These complementary features drive a fuzzy inference system (FIS) that adaptively adjusts the kernel width to balance outlier suppression and maneuver responsiveness. Subsequent measurements within the window guide the update of a past state, yielding a fixed-lag smoothing scheme. Simulations involving four low-Earth-orbit satellites tracking a maneuvering high-altitude space target under impulsive measurement contamination demonstrate substantially improved position estimation. With a fixed lag of 10 steps, the proposed smoother achieves time-averaged position and velocity root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 13.14 m and 0.1165 m/s over the final 200 s, respectively.

With a fixed lag of 10 steps, the proposed smoother achieves time-averaged position and velocity root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 13.14 m and 0.1165 m/s over the final 200 s, respectively.

title: Most Colon Grading Mistakes Are Neighbors: Adjacent-Grade Error Shares and Grade-3 Recall on Public Histopathology Embeddings
abstract: Colon histology computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) papers often lead with pooled grading accuracy. That number mixes easy majority-class hits with minority-class misses and treats a Grade 1↔Grade 2 swap as interchangeable with calling poorly differentiated cancer well differentiated. This preprint recomputes stratified five-fold support-vector grading on 560 public colorectal cancer patches with frozen ResNet50 embeddings (Grade 1 n=251, Grade 2 n=210, Grade 3 n=99). Cross-validated accuracy is 73.6% ± 2.9% and macro-F1 is 0.705, but Grade 3 recall is only 0.475. Of 148 residual mistakes, 119 (80.4%) are adjacent-grade swaps; 29 (19.6%) jump from Grade 3 to Grade 1. A published soft-voting ensemble confusion matrix shows the same structure: 86.0% of errors remain adjacent. We treat that adjacent share as the checkable claim—not a new leaderboard—and argue that Grade 3 recall and adjacent versus non-adjacent error counts should be reported before pooled accuracy is read as a deployment summary. Embedding protocol and ensemble confusion-matrix anchors follow a published two-stage colon pipeline; no new patients were enrolled.

title: The exact worst-case asymptotic rate of Nesterov acceleration for strongly convex optimization
abstract: We study Nesterov's accelerated gradient method with its standard constant parameters for smooth strongly convex optimization. We characterize the exact worst-case asymptotic factor for the squared distance to the minimizer. To this end, we construct candidate worst-case trajectories by combining planar spirals with a common contraction factor that satisfy a self-similarity condition. Each component rotates by a fixed angle at every iteration. The exact factor is the optimal value of a linear optimization problem over probability measures on a fixed disk, with constraints derived from smooth strongly convex interpolation. Every optimal measure has a common contraction factor, which is also the largest factor for which the angular interpolation conditions are feasible. We also show that this worst-case asymptotic rate can be realized by a \emph{single} function in a finite-dimensional space whose iterates attain this factor. A matching upper bound holds uniformly over all functions in the class and all finite dimensions. Consequently, allowing the function, dimension, and initial point to vary with the iteration horizon does not increase the worst-case asymptotic factor. We also show that the exact factor is $1-4/(3\sqrtκ)+o(κ^{-1/2})$ as $κ\to\infty$, where $κ=L/μ$ is the ratio of the gradient Lipschitz constant to the strong convexity parameter.

title: Metric-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Object Hallucination Reduction in LVLM-Based Image Captioning
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.

title: Trinity / Trinitas: A Complete Record of Five Months Teaching a Small Liquid-Substrate System to Speak on One 24 GB Workstation — Architecture, Instrument Culture, Results, Failures, and Retractions
abstract: A complete measured record (May–October 2026) of building and training a from-scratch liquid-substrate research system — a 331 M-parameter CfC/τ-band predictive world model and three ~27 M-parameter recurrent language policies — on a single Quadro RTX 6000 (24 GB, no hardware bf16), with no prebuilt weights and no human-preference RLHF. The failures are reported at the same weight as the successes: a foundation run that read 0.3 % of its corpus; three speakers pretrained bit-identical; a reward blind to its own speakers' collapse; a pre-registered n = 3 replication measuring a 44.6-point spread across identical configurations; a CfC language core shown to be a tied-gate GRU without Δt, with a shuffled-Δt control establishing that the gate is live to time. Dialogue SFT gave +8.2 points (correcting an earlier +16.3); decode-time constraints alone gave +16.3 with zero spread. The system does not yet pass a Phase-1 graduation epoch, and the paper says so on page one. The contribution is methodological — gauges certified by negative arms, pre-registered criteria, replication before conclusion, and a ledger of 44 retractions preserved in full — with the headline section pre-registered and left empty for the run it waits on.

title: A complete classification of operator controllability for closed three-level quantum systems driven by a single control
abstract: In this work, we study operator controllability of finite-dimensional closed quantum systems driven by a single coherent control. Two general Lie-algebraic results on controllability of such systems are proved. The first gives sufficient conditions under which controllability of the system is preserved when controlled energy-level shifts are added. The second gives a sufficient basis-element condition under which the dynamical Lie algebra contains $\mathfrak{su}(N)$ and the system is therefore operator controllable. These results, together with known controllability conditions, are applied to obtain a complete classification of operator controllability of all three-level quantum systems in terms of their free and interaction Hamiltonian matrix elements. This classification covers all combinations of energy-level and level-spacing degeneracies, two or three allowed transitions, as well as the presence or absence of controlled energy-level shifts, and gives necessary and sufficient conditions for operator controllability in each case.

title: LYNX: Analytical Program Synthesis via Grounding and Closed-Loop Refinement
abstract: LLM-powered data analytics aims to translate natural language instructions into executable analytical programs over underlying data. However, existing approaches, whether treating LLMs as intent-to-code translators or as standalone analytical engines, often fail to reliably align domain semantics with complex schemas and heterogeneous metadata, resulting in brittle execution and semantically inconsistent analytical outputs in real-world workloads. We present LYNX, a multi-agent framework that formulates LLM-driven analytics as a schema- and knowledge-constrained analysis problem rather than a single-pass generation task. LYNX organizes analytical synthesis into a closed-loop workflow of planning, generation, verification, and refinement through three role-specialized agents that collaboratively enforce schema grounding, semantic consistency, and execution correctness. To address domain ambiguity and schema misalignment, LYNX integrates Semantic-Structural Distillation and Stage-Aware Allocation (SSD-SAA). A delta-guided iterative revision continuously diagnoses and repairs semantic and execution-level failures, substantially improving synthesis robustness. We evaluate LYNX on two NL-to-SQL benchmarks, BIRD-SQL Mini-Dev and the more challenging Spider 2.0-Lite. Experimental results demonstrate strong performance and efficiency, achieving 10.66% to 59.54% execution accuracy across lightweight and commercial models, while reducing token consumption by 70.53% compared with the prior most efficient method. Our framework displays high generalization over different backbones, from open-source, lightweight models to the latest commercial models. Additional case studies on quantitative finance analytics and complex multi-relational SQL workloads further demonstrate the framework's robustness, scalability, and practical applicability in real-world analytical scenarios.

title: Self-improving data synthesis enables scalable adaptation of embedding models
abstract: AI agents require specialised retrieval across domains and tasks, but adapting embedding models is constrained by costly manual training-data design. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a self-improving agentic framework that turns a few retrieval examples into reusable synthesis instructions. Given an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs, SYNTRA infers implicit information needs and relevance criteria, then uses feedback on trial outputs to refine instructions for query generation and relevance assessment. Experiments across 24 datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate that the same synthesis workflow produces effective training data, benefiting even strong embedding models with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement strengthens this supervision on all six evaluated tasks, yielding better retrieval than human calibration on four. The training value persists at larger scales: on MS MARCO, retrieval gains continue across a 32-fold range of synthetic training-data sizes. SYNTRA thus enables scalable embedding-model adaptation with minimal human intervention.

title: Fading Memory and Nonlinear Dynamics in a Microring Resonator Network and their Use in Computation: data-analysis files
abstract: Fading Memory and Nonlinear Dynamics in a Microring Resonator Network and their Use in Computation: data-analysis files This archive contains the Python files used for data analysis in the paper that links to this repository.It is a minimal source-code snapshot prepared for Zenodo; datasets, generated caches, figures, and local environments are not included. The code is provided as is, and successful execution is not guaranteed.Paths will probably need to be adjusted to your local data layout and working environment.The scripts have not been run or tested as a standalone archive. Structure .├── README.md├── pyproject.toml # Dependencies and build configuration├── uv.lock # Locked dependency versions├── .python-version├── src/rf_memory_lovers/ # Basic functions for data loading and analysis├── mains/ # Long-running data-analysis routines└── visual/ # Figure production, visualization, and reporting ├── about_0intro/ ├── about_fft/ ├── about_mc/ ├── about_NARMA/ └── helpers/ `src/rf_memory_lovers/` contains the basic functions used by the analysis `mains/` contains the long-running routines that carry out the data analysis. `visual/` contains code for producing figures, visualizations, and analysis reports, together with the required shared helpers. Environment and data Use Python 3.12 or later.From this archive's root, install the locked environment with `uv sync --locked --extra cpu`; use `--extra cu128` instead for the CUDA 12.8 PyTorch configuration.Choose one PyTorch extra, not both. Run entry scripts as modules from this root, for example `uv run --no-sync python -m mains.main_singleports` or `uv run --no-sync python -m visual.about_mc.plot_ports`, so the root-level `mains` and `visual` namespace packages are importable. The data used by this analysis are already preprocessed using scripts available in a separate project: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17105607 The corresponding preprocessed inputs must be supplied separately.Many figures also require previously generated analysis caches.In particular, check the paths in `src/rf_memory_lovers/paths.py` and any input/output paths in the routines you intend to use; they will probably need adjustment for your environment.This archive alone does not contain all inputs needed to reproduce the results. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request.The dataset comprises several hundred gigabytes and is not included in this source-code archive. Julia simulations The Julia files used to run the simulations are not currently included.They are part of an evolving project and will eventually be published in a more appropriate location.They are available from the authors on request.The Python simulation-plotting script also requires the separate simulation outputs.
