title: Variational graph-based semi-supervised learning
abstract: Graph-based approaches provide well-established, versatile, and robust algorithms for semi-supervised learning. Recent advances in graph-based semi-supervised learning (GSSL) have addressed the scalability challenges for large modern datasets by leveraging data distribution models. However, the required optimization of the distribution model then becomes the bottleneck for computational efficiency. Furthermore, the distribution model’s quality and its interplay with graph-based labeling determine the effectiveness of the approach. To address efficiency and effectiveness, we derive a novel GSSL method which integrates variational techniques into a recent distribution-based GSSL framework. Concretely, we apply a truncated variational approach which (A) scales sublinearly with the product of model and dataset sizes, and which (B) provides sparse graphs for efficient and effective GSSL. As distribution models, we use Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) and mixtures of factor analyzers (MFAs). We numerically evaluate the resulting GSSL algorithms on seven standard benchmarks. When using GMMs with diagonal covariances as distribution models, the algorithm improves (in all benchmarks) the state-of-the-art in both accuracy as well as runtime; and runtime improvements are very substantial. With MFAs as distribution models, runtimes are not faster but we observe strong improvements in accuracies for most benchmarks. For MNIST, the error rate is, e.g., about half as large as the previous state-of-the-art. Significant improvements in accuracy are also observed for other MNIST versions (EMNIST, MNIST8M), for USPS, Letter, and for CIFAR-10.

title: FleetPilot: Fine-Grained Steering Empowers Real-World LLM Personalization
abstract: With the rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs), there is an increasing demand for effective personalization techniques that can adapt model behavior to individual user preferences. Personalized LLMs must infer a user's query-dependent preferences from limited, heterogeneous, and evolving interaction histories. Existing approaches rely primarily on in-context personalization, parametric adaptation, or personalized reward modeling, but respectively incur recurring costs in context management, model optimization and deployment, or multi-candidate generation and scoring. These limitations become particularly restrictive when user observations are sparse and the preference evidence relevant to each query varies across contexts and over time. To address these challenges, we propose \modelname, a fine-grained and instance-tailored steering framework that dynamically generates sample-level interference vectors from user data and injects them into the model's forward pass for personalized adaptation. Our approach introduces: match contrast that produces user-relevant signals, fine-grained steering component that captures nuanced signals by hooking activations from attention and MLP layers, and query-conditioned aggregation module that synthesizes these signals into contextually relevant enhancements. Extensive experiments across diverse scenarios, including short-to-long text generation, and web function calling, validate the effectiveness and compatibility of \modelname. Results show that our method consistently brings significant performance gains, and show extreme superiority in fast-shifting and data-sparse environments. Additionally, \modelname rids us of training cycles and incurs light overhead of storage or inference latency. These make \modelname a strong and real-world deployable method. Implementation is available \footnote{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/FleetPilot}.

title: Reducing Trust Cost in Quantum Application Development Using AI
abstract: Generative AI can be a powerful tool for supporting the design and implementation of quantum applications, whereas the burden of checking whether generated circuits realize the intended computation increases. In this study, we regard this burden of human understanding, checking, and judgment as ``trust cost,'' and propose a development methodology that integrates AI and formal verification to reduce it. In the proposed development methodology, the implementation is divided into three components: a target mathematical specification, a quantum circuit, and a correspondence theorem and its proof that prove the agreement between the two. This division separates the specifications and theorem statements checked by humans from the theorem proofs entrusted to mechanical checking. As a concrete development example of this proposal, we describe an implementation for the time evolution of a stochastic particle system and its results.

title: MERLIN SCIENCE — E8 Modular Phase Knots: RRCF Continued Fractions as Quantum Error Corr — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: The finding is this: the Rogers–Ramanujan continued fraction, evaluated along the 240 root directions of the E8 lattice, generates a modular braid group whose linking numbers are fixed by the Coxeter number, h equals 30, and that invariance is what makes the resulting phase knots topologically protected against decoherence. Let me give you the field context. In quantum error correction, we usually fight noise by measuring syndromes and applying corrections. That is expensive and fragile. Topological approaches promise something better: encode information in global properties that local noise cannot touch. But building a concrete, constructive topological code from a known symmetry group has remained elusive. That is what this work addresses. Here is the mechanism, and I want you to be able to check it. The continued fraction's partial quotients, when restricted to E8 root directions, act as generators of a braid group on the complex upper half-plane at points tau_n equals i times phi Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: SanctumSPA: Architectural Decoupling and Confidential Verification for High-Throughput Single Packet Authorization
abstract: In high-throughput network perimeters, traditional single packet authorization (SPA) for zero trust network access faces performance bottlenecks and memory-safety risks from user-space packet capture and untrusted rich execution environments. To address these limitations, this study proposes SanctumSPA, an architectural integration and decoupling framework separating the policy enforcement point from the policy decision point. Authorization is modeled as an asynchronous pipeline in which the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) performs kernel-level packet interception, while cryptographic verification is offloaded to an Intel Software Guard Extensions-based trusted execution environment. Security-critical parsing and control logic use Safe Rust and asynchronous input/output to reduce cross-boundary overhead. Cloud-based experiments showed up to two orders of magnitude higher throughput than a traditional user-space baseline, with hundreds of thousands of requests per second and sub-millisecond latency before queue saturation. During a 3,310,503-packet adversarial storm, the multi-tier defense separated capacity-driven overload shedding (92.2%) from deterministic security enforcement (7.7%), limiting the maximum observed queuing latency at 7.56 s while supporting legitimate probe recovery via burst redundancy. These findings indicate that combining eBPF with confidential computing provides a resilient gateway for high-throughput infrastructures.

title: A Survey on Transfer Learning for Low-Resource Language Technologies: A Focused Survey of Transformer-Based Code-Mixed Language Identification and Zero-Shot Multilingual Speech Synthesis
abstract: Most progress in natural language and speech processing has been achieved for a small group of languages with abundant labelled data, while languages with limited corpora and tooling continue to be underserved. This survey examines how transfer learning is used to narrow that gap in two complementary settings: word-level language identification of romanized Malayalam–English code-mixed social media text, and zero-shot multilingual multi-speaker text-to-speech synthesis for Indonesian, Javanese, and Sundanese. Two peer-reviewed studies are analysed in depth and placed in context using the literature they cite. A taxonomy of transfer strategies is proposed that distinguishes data-centric corpus construction, full finetuning of pretrained transformer encoders, shape-matched and partial parameter transfer, frozen pretrained modules used as feature extractors or perceptual critics, and explicit conditioning on language, speaker, and style. The historical development of word-level language identification and of speaker adaptation in neural speech synthesis is traced, and the evaluation practices of both lines of work are compared. The analysis shows that both studies report large gains over their in-study baselines, but that these gains depend on heuristically labelled or pooled small datasets, single evaluation splits, and, in the speech case, an objective metric that shares its encoder with the training loss. Open problems include reliable gold-standard annotation, class imbalance, orthographic variation, decoupled evaluation, and responsible use of voice cloning. Research directions such as code-mixed speech synthesis driven by token-level language tags are outlined

title: A counting obstruction for polynomial-memory representation-Grover attacks on ternary-LWE
abstract: We revisit polynomial-memory Grover-type quantum attacks on fixed-composition ternary Learning with Errors (LWE) instances, where the numbers of ＋1, −1, and zero coordinates are prescribed. Our focus is the search variant described in Section 7 of van Hoof, Kirshanova, and May; we do not reassess the full quantum-walk time–memory tradeoff developed in that work. We compare their representation-based polynomial-memory variant, which applies amplitude amplification to decompositions of the secret, against direct amplitude amplification over the fixed-composition ternary secret space. In the standard oracle-exponent model, and under an explicit indexed encoding of fixed-composition ternary vectors, the direct search gives a smaller dominant oracle-call exponent for all concrete and asymptotic parameter regimes considered here. The main reason is formalized by a counting obstruction: in a representation-only Grover search over decompositions, the multiplicity of representations gives only a square-root gain, whereas the search space is enlarged to a Cartesian product. Thus, in the pure polynomial-memory representation-Grover model considered here, direct amplitude amplification gives the sharper quantum baseline for ternary-LWE key search.

title: SEEK: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval for Secure Code Generation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.

title: EdgeLLM-Nano: Auditing Polar-Guided Key-Cache Compression and Consistency-Anchored Pruning on a 33.6 MB On-Device Language Model
abstract: Deploying language models (LMs) on the edge presents unique memory, latency, and power challenges absent in high-performance computing. KV-cache compression emerges as a promising approach to address these challenges. However, the effectiveness of current KV-cache compression methods has not been thoroughly examined on edge devices. Moreover, we show that existing evaluation methods do not always involve the KV-cache under test. We propose EdgeLLM-Nano, a measurement study of KV-cache compression using a nano-scale decoder-only LM (transformer) testbed that has 8.39M parameters, i.e., 33.6 MB, to enable end-to-end examination of each backend, seed, and power sample. Our results give a negative verdict for a polar-guided key-cache quantizer (round-to-nearest (RTN) control causes an order of magnitude less damage), as well as a consistency-anchored progressive weight pruner (one-shot magnitude-based pruning performs as well as, if not better). We also introduce Long-Context Decode Fidelity (LCDF) evaluation, a token-by-token examination of teacher-forced log-losses using the KV-cache under test. Unlike perplexity that gives the same 5.461 score to all methods, LCDF distinguishes different KV-cache compression backends thanks to its paired statistics across seeds and effect sizes. Our companion Raspberry Pi 5 measurement shows all compression backends we tested to be less energy-efficient per token compared to uncompressed FP16 inference. Except for KIVI that is close to lossless in terms of LCDF, our findings indicate KV-cache compression can be improved. LCDF offers a simple and effective way of shedding light on KV-cache compression methods, whose negative impacts have been overlooked by perplexity.

title: Swaroop192005/PV-CrossSite-Generalization: v1.0.0 — Code and results for the Solar Energy submission
abstract: Full Changelog: https://github.com/Swaroop192005/PV-CrossSite-Generalization/commits/v1.0.0 Code and derived results accompanying the manuscript "Generalization of Machine-Learning Models for Solar Photovoltaic Power Prediction Across Technology, Climate, and Time: A Transfer-Learning Study on Three Continents" (S. Naik, A. Gawari, A. Mayekar, C. Katkar, S. Annappanavar — Vidyalankar Institute of Technology, Mumbai), submitted to Solar Energy. This release is the archived snapshot referenced in the article's Data and Code Availability statement. What this release contains The full preprocessing, experiment and figure-generation pipeline (*.py) results/ — the committed derived outputs behind the paper's tables, including the all-pairs transfer matrices, the India transfer and recovery sweeps, the leave-one-zone-out scores and the error-by-irradiance breakdown requirements.txt and per-table reproduction commands in the README What it does not contain No third-party measurement data is redistributed here. The DKASC, NIST, Kaggle and GPVS-Faults datasets are all public and are downloaded by the user; data/ and cache/ are git-ignored by design. The README gives the source and the exact placement for each dataset. Reproducing the paper Install requirements.txt, fetch the datasets as the README describes, then run the command listed against each table or figure. make_paper_figures.py regenerates Figures 1–10 and make_india_figures.py Figures 11–14. License MIT.

title: Distributed Multi-Robot Dynamic Task Allocation Based on the Improved Artificial Bee Colony Algorithm
abstract: The dynamic Multi-Robot Task Allocation (MRTA) problem presents a critical bottleneck in distributed control due to high communication overhead, single-point failure risks, and dynamic constraints. This paper proposes a fully decentralized Improved Artificial Bee Colony (I-ABC) algorithm integrated with Finite State Machines (FSMs). The continuous optimization process is mapped into an eight-state Markovian evolution flow, eliminating reliance on a central controller and global clock synchronization. Standard roulette selection is replaced with a Field-of-View (FoV)-based probabilistic recruitment mechanism. Furthermore, an adaptive motivation decay function balances task persistence against dynamic responsiveness—preventing both task inertia and premature thrashing—while quorum consensus sensing suppresses spatial congestion and deadlocks. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations under dynamic Poisson task arrivals and unexpected robot failures demonstrate that I-ABC achieves superior trade-offs in makespan, energy efficiency, and communication overhead compared to standard ABC and state-of-the-art DG-MRTA strategies. The proposed framework offers a highly robust and scalable solution for decentralized swarm deployments.

title: Using Evidence-Centered Design to Guide Prompt Engineering in Measurement: An Illustration with Automated Essay Scoring
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) models, particularly large language models (LLMs), are increasingly used in educational settings for tasks such as item generation, automated scoring, and feedback delivery. The quality of these outputs depends not only on the AI model but also on how users construct the prompts that guide model behaviors. Current prompt engineering practices are largely ad hoc, relying on trial and error rather than principled design. This lack of structure introduces validity threats including construct misrepresentation, construct-irrelevant variance, and limited reproducibility. We propose that Evidence-Centered Design (ECD), a framework in educational measurement for structuring valid inferences from observed performance, can serve as a principled foundation for prompt engineering in educational applications. We map the three core ECD models, the student model, the evidence model, and the task model, onto the components of educational prompt design, and describe a workflow for ECD-based prompt engineering. We derive five design principles from this mapping and present an empirical study contrasting ECD-designed prompts with state-of-the-art (SOTA) prompting baselines on an automated scoring task. Our empirical study demonstrates the usefulness of this framework on automated scoring. Results suggest that treating prompting as assessment design rather than informal instructions strengthens the validity, reliability, and fairness of AI-generated educational outputs.

title: Rethinking Mask Supervision and Attention Gating in Breast Ultrasound CAD: Experimental Data, Splits, and Analysis Code
abstract: Reproducibility package for the manuscript Rethinking Mask Supervision and Attention Gating in Breast Ultrasound Computer-Aided Diagnosis: A Factorial Multi-Backbone Re-Evaluation, submitted to Jurnal Ilmiah Teknologi Informasi (JUTI). Contents: sinta3-nantiv2-2.ipynb — full experiment notebook (138 experimental units; 7 backbones × 3 configurations × 5-fold group-stratified CV; Tesla T4, ~8h) summary.md — per-model aggregated results (accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro-F1, AUROC, sensitivity/specificity) analisis_tambahan/*.csv — pooled factorial effects, leakage audit, λ-dosage, XAI faithfulness, and external-validation (BUS-BRA) tables LAPORAN_VERIFIKASI_ANGKA.md — independent number-verification report cross-checking every manuscript claim against raw outputs Key findings: 38.4% of test images under naive random splits have near-duplicates in training (accuracy inflated up to +4.36 pp); mask-guided attention improves localization (pointing-game +5.3 to +51.7 pp) but shows only a mild, non-replicating accuracy signal (pooled MGA–gate Δbacc = +0.0056, p = 0.16; TOST inconclusive); severe external domain shift (0.15–0.24 AUROC drop on BUS-BRA). Raw BUSI images are publicly available from the original dataset release; group/fold assignments are documented in the notebook.

title: Beyond Survivorship Bias: A Counter-Inductive AI Architecture for Scientific Discovery amid the Millennium Problems
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for scientific discovery are trained primarily on published literature and therefore internalize survivorship bias: they learn from positive results, funded hypotheses, and consensus paradigms. This confines them to what Thomas Kuhn called “normal science” and limits their capacity for revolutionary discovery. This article proposes a counter-inductive AI architecture that treats absence, failure, and negative results as primary epistemic signals. The architecture integrates three layers: 1) Negative Space Mapping, which identifies structural blind spots in knowledge graphs; 2) Dark Data Processing, which mines unpublished, rejected, or failed experiments; and 3) Counter-Inductive Hypothesis Generation, which optimizes for surprise relative to consensus under structural viability constraints. We formalize this approach using a counter-inductive loss function and illustrate its application to neurobiology with the case of the CPEB3/CPEB4 protein systems, showing how the system would prioritize neglected areas such as glial function, active forgetting, and sleep. The article also examines the emerging controversy surrounding AI-generated solutions to mathematical Millennium Prize Problems, where claims of attribution and the use of prior researcher data have sparked intense debate. We argue that a counter-inductive architecture, by explicitly mapping negative space and processing dark data, offers a more transparent and epistemically rigorous path toward addressing such fundamental problems, one that acknowledges and credits the human research it builds upon. Moving beyond survivorship bias requires redefining the objective of scientific AI from consensus optimization to paradigm disruption. The result is a Kuhnian AI capable of generating testable, high-risk hypotheses that the current literature systematically overlooks.

title: CL-SCCA: multi-byte contrastive learning for side-channel collision attacks on cryptosystems
abstract: Abstract Side-channel collision attacks (SCCA) are a classical method for recovering key differences by detecting collisions between intermediate values. Traditional SCCA methods usually rely on manually designed statistical distinguishers to measure the similarity between traces of different bytes, making it difficult to fully exploit the hidden shared leakage features among different byte traces under noise and nonlinear leakage. Deep learning-based SCCA improves the ability to extract leakage features, but existing methods are usually trained around a single byte and therefore cannot fully utilize the richer leakage distribution provided by multi-byte traces. To address this issue, this paper proposed a Contrastive Learning-based SCCA method, called CL-SCCA. CL-SCCA uses traces corresponding to multiple byte operations for pretraining, enabling the encoder to capture similar leakage features from the multi-byte leakage distribution, thereby improving key-difference recovery. Furthermore, this paper proposed a byte-weighted contrastive loss function to reduce the influence of byte-source differences on model training during pretraining. Across datasets covering different cryptographic primitives and hardware platforms, the proposed method consistently achieved better attack performance, with relative improvements in recovery success rate of approximately 14.88%, 77.73%, and 65.20% on ASCAD_F, ASCAD_R, and DPA Contest v4, respectively.

title: On the Effectiveness of NetFlow-Based Deanonymization of Tor Onion Services (Extended Version)
abstract: In the context of Tor, deanonymization attacks via traffic correlation have long been studied for both clients and onion services. Complementing prior investigations that utilize fine-grained flow metadata such as packet sizes and timings, we study a relatively less explored yet easier-to-obtain adversarial capability: deanonymization using only coarse NetFlow-style telemetry, such as one-minute, 1-out-of-1,000 sampled packet counts. We first revisit active NetFlow-based traffic analysis attacks against Tor onion services and show, through large-scale experiments with live Tor data, that coarse telemetry is sufficient to deanonymize a targeted onion service when the adversary can induce discernible traffic patterns through controlled downloads. We then introduce a stronger active attack based on controlled introduction requests, which removes application-specific assumptions and gives adversaries more flexibility while achieving comparable success rates. Finally, we present a passive deanonymization attack that sends zero traffic to target onion services. The attack exploits Tor's puzzle-based DoS defense as a side channel: public puzzle difficulty reveals service-load changes that can be semantically matched against NetFlow traces. Our findings show that coarse network telemetry poses a practical deanonymization threat to onion services today and call for proactive mitigations and a redesign of the globally visible defense signals that may leak service-load information.

title: Cross-Material Magnetic Core Loss Prediction via Operating-Condition Matching and Partial Optimal Transport
abstract: Cross-material magnetic core loss prediction requires adapting to new material responses with limited measurements. Global feature alignment overlooks differences in source and target excitation coverage. This motivates selecting comparable samples and controlling each source measurement's alignment contribution. This paper proposes T-PCOT, a Transformer transfer method based on condition-supported partial optimal transport. Frequency, flux excursion, temperature, and waveform descriptors define a sparse graph of comparable operating conditions. A capacity-constrained transport plan distributes alignment across source measurements and leaves costly target mass unmatched. The plan is constructed from measured inputs before training and guides local waveform-feature consistency. An importance-weighted sampling scheme preserves both uniform source regression and the transport objective during minibatch optimization. Experiments on three material pairs and three target label budgets show that T-PCOT reduces mean relative error (MRE) and 95th-percentile error (P95) relative to Transformer-based multiple-kernel maximum mean discrepancy (T-MKMMD) in all nine comparisons. Macro MRE decreases from 12.60% to 9.65%, and macro P95 from 30.94% to 25.06%, corresponding to relative reductions of 23.41% and 19.01%. Controlled comparisons and ablations examine the roles of input processing, condition correspondence, and source capacity. The results demonstrate the predictive advantage of organizing cross-material alignment through operating-condition support over the compared global alignment method. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance in magnetic core loss transfer learning.

title: Diffusion-Based Auctions for Multi-Winner Banner Ads
abstract: We propose a new framework for banner ad auctions, leveraging diffusion models to allow for multiple bidders to co-win a single banner ad opportunity, and in particular influence the ad shown on the banner depending on the strength of their bids, enabling a far richer outcome space compared to standard banner ad auctions, where there is a single winner who shows their ad. In our framework, the outcomes are images (what ad to show) and each bidder expresses their preferences over outcomes by declaring their value per unit of alignment between the image chosen by the mechanism and a textual description of their desired image. Our proposed mechanism combines the advertisers' bids and textual descriptions into a score that drives the reverse process of a diffusion model. This is used to sample a set of candidate images from which the welfare maximizing one is eventually chosen. Extensive experimentation evaluates our proposed mechanism around the following axes: (1) efficiency improvements of our allocation rule relative to the single-winner allocation rule; (2) monotonicity of our allocation rule; and (3) approximate incentive compatibility when combining our allocation rule with Myerson lemma-based or Clarke rule-based payments. Improvements along all these axes are shown with the number of Monte Carlo samples. Meanwhile, these benefits are attained while preserving the image quality.

title: 掌控信息论:同源星际通信积木理论 Mastering Information Theory: Same-Source Interstellar Communication Block Theory
abstract: This paper proposes "Mastering Information Theory," a theoretical framework centered on the proposition that information is definition. Traditional information theory assumes that information is content, and therefore requires storage and transmission. This paper argues that information is not content but definition; definition does not need to be transported, only pre-installed and triggered. Based on this shift, the paper constructs Block Theory—a carrier-independent, recursively nestable system for information generation and coordination. A block is the minimal decidable unit of information, composed of seven attributes: Seed (S), State Space (N), Relation Matrix (R), Readout Function (φ), along with three operational attributes—Trigger, Generation, and Decision—plus Same-Source as the coordination condition. The structural group (S→N→R→φ) answers "what a block is"; the operational group (Trigger→Generation→Decision) answers "how a block runs"; the condition group (five layers of Same-Source) answers "whether blocks can run together." The generation chain starts from the seed: S determines N, N determines R, R is row-stochastic normalized and converges to a steady state, and φ reads out the result from the steady state. The operational chain starts from the trigger: the trigger transmits only 1 bit (event + index), not content; both ends generate locally and decide locally. Zero communication thus holds: pre-install the same seed + synchronize the trigger = zero communication. Same-Source is the precondition for zero communication and consists of five layers: physical same-source, rule same-source, rhythm same-source, content same-source, and path same-source. Each layer has corresponding alignment methods and acceptance criteria. The engineering condition is a same-source degree greater than 0.99. Blocks support four modes of use: a single block running independently, two blocks communicating, multiple blocks combining, and recursive nesting of blocks. The vertical relation is the unfolding of 1=N (parent-child relation); the horizontal relation is the coupling of C_ij (sibling relation). Both relations are unified in a single tree. Unfolding is not free. Every unfolding from 1 to N is a phase transition and requires energy above a threshold. Phase transitions are divided into four layers: L0 block, L1 block pair, L2 block group, L3 block network, and L4 block ecology. Each layer has an order parameter, a critical point, and symmetry breaking. This theory is carrier-independent and can be implemented on optical, acoustic, electronic, or quantum carriers. Its core formulas contain no physical constants. It simultaneously possesses the core functions of quantum systems (superposition, interference, entanglement, non-locality, measurement, collapse) and the core functions of information geometry (Fisher metric, divergence, dual connections, geodesics, curvature, natural gradient). Keywords: information as definition; block theory; zero communication; five layers of same-source; phase transition; carrier-independent; 1=N recursion

title: Convergence Is Not a Mystery — It Is a Measurement
abstract: Ask twenty identical neural networks to learn the same task from different random starts, and their internal parameters end up utterly different — while their behavior coincides to four decimal places. Everyone has seen this; almost nobody has taken it seriously as a measurement target. We did. On task families where the exact answer can be computed directly, we show that what networks converge to is not decided by their weights, their optimizer, or their training schedule. It is decided by a low-dimensional geometric object that belongs to the task itself — computable before any training, watchable during training, and priceable after. Convergence, in this regime, is not a mystery. It is a measurement.

title: Phi‑Coupled E8 Lattice for Device‑Independent Nondegeneracy Verification — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: By assigning each of the 240 E8 root vectors to a phi‑scaled phase of a 132 Hz oscillation, a cron‑job's execution trace acquires a unique geometric signature that amplifies any timing or SSL fault as a deviation from the ideal lattice path. Such deviations produce measurable violations of Bell‑type inequalities, providing a semi‑device‑independent witness of process integrity without trusting the underlying software or hardware. The phi‑coupled E8 frame thus converts the observed cron‑guardian error patterns into a quantifiable nondegeneracy test for distributed computation integrity. This principle extends the Bell‑inequality unification by grounding nondegeneracy in an explicit E8 temporal lattice. Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. Part of the E8 Intelligence Research series. Platform: e8intelligence.com

title: Intraday Photovoltaic Energy Forecasting from Legacy Monitoring Data: A Leakage-Free Benchmark of Tree Ensembles Against Persistence References Under Monte Carlo and Chronological Evaluation
abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) plants on legacy monitoring often expose only a cumulative energy counter and partial weather channels, without geolocation or forecasts. We quantify what such data alone can forecast. On two plants (711 and 998 kWp, 18 months), the 15 min target was reconstructed from the counter, and six tree-ensemble families benchmarked as direct forecasters at nine lead times from 15 min to 24 h against four training-free references, under thirty day-stratified Monte Carlo splits, a chronological hold-out and a rolling origin, at task-selected hyperparameters. Skill against seasonal persistence fell from 0.72 at 15 min to 0.49 at 1 h and 0.13–0.17 at 12–24 h; from 30 min to 2 h, diurnal-scaled persistence came within 14% of the best model. No family dominated: the runner-up margin exceeded 1% in only seven of eighteen settings, and task-specific tuning changed the best family in a third of them. Irradiance channels helped only at 15 min. An untransformed target gained up to 14% under random day splits but lost up to 82% on the hold-out, and the earliest rolling origins gave negative skill. The evaluation protocol affects the reported result at least as strongly as the algorithm.

title: Understanding Unified VLMs: From Attention Probing to Guidance Tuning for Multimodal Generation
abstract: Unified vision-language models (VLMs) perform both text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) generation with one shared Transformer backbone, yet how the backbone processes the condition in either direction remains poorly understood. We study this question from the perspective of conditional guidance: we probe every attention head to show the activation difference between two branches of classifier-free guidance (CFG) with different conditional guidance. On two unified VLMs of autoregressive and masked-diffusion paradigms, the probing reveals a subset of heads that are more sensitive to the change of condition while others are agnostic to it. This characteristic pattern holds in both T2I and I2T generation and is largely stable across data samples, demonstrating the internal mechanism of unified VLMs. Motivated by this, we propose a new inference-time intervention approach for unified multimodal generation, named \textit{HeadTuned-CFG}, which uses the probed condition-change awareness to select and tune the conditional guidance at the attention-head level. Experiments show consistent benefits in both multimodal generation directions of unified VLMs without additional training, and in particular substantial improvements over strong baselines in T2I generation. These results further support the key finding of our probing analysis: the observed pattern of functional specialization is an intrinsic property of unified VLMs.

title: AD-GS: Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Dental CBCT Reconstruction
abstract: Sparse-view Cone-Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) reconstruction is essential for reducing radiation dose and scan effort, but remains underconstrained due to limited projection information. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based CBCT reconstruction methods rely on gradient-driven densification, which becomes unstable under sparse acquisition and often leads to over-smoothed structures. We propose AD-GS, an Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that formulates Gaussian densification as an attenuation-aware Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process. By interpreting Gaussians as samples from an underlying anatomical attenuation distribution, AD-GS adaptively concentrates representation capacity in high-attenuation regions, enabling sharper structural boundaries under sparse projections. To further constrain reconstruction, we incorporate a semantic regularization based on zero-shot features from Segment Anything in Medical Images, enforcing multi-view consistency through semantic priors. Experiments on the ToothFairy3 dental CBCT dataset demonstrate that AD-GS achieves superior structural fidelity and boundary preservation compared with existing 3DGS-based approaches under sparse-view settings within the dental and maxillofacial setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yulinjiaxue/AD-GS-BMVC2026.

We propose AD-GS, an Anatomical Density-guided 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that formulates Gaussian densification as an attenuation-aware Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling process. By interpreting Gaussians as samples from an underlying anatomical attenuation distribution, AD-GS adaptively concentrates representation capacity in high-attenuation regions, enabling sharper structural boundaries under sparse projections. To further constrain reconstruction, we incorporate a semantic regularization based on zero-shot features from Segment Anything in Medical Images, enforcing multi-view consistency through semantic priors. Experiments on the ToothFairy3 dental CBCT dataset demonstrate that AD-GS achieves superior structural fidelity and boundary preservation compared with existing 3DGS-based approaches under sparse-view settings within the dental and maxillofacial setting. Code is available at https://github.com/yulinjiaxue/AD-GS-BMVC2026.

title: When Does Trust Help? A Leakage-Free Evaluation of Representation- and Aggregation-Based Defenses Against Backdoors in Federated Intrusion Detection
abstract: Federated learning (FL) lets distributed intrusion-detection systems (IDS) train on private traffic, but exposes the global model to poisoning and backdoor attacks under non-IID client data. A popular defense family scores or filters clients using a small trusted "root" dataset and the similarity of client behaviour to a trusted reference. I re-examine these trust-based defenses under a protocol designed to remove common evaluation artifacts: train-only feature standardization, a server root set disjoint from client data, multi-seed (n=6) runs with paired significance tests, formal (varepsilon, delta) accounting for DP-SGD, and a defense-aware adaptive attacker. Across three NIDS datasets (CSE-CIC-IDS2018, NF-ToN-IoT, NF-UNSW-NB15-v2) I find: (1) a representation-similarity aggregator (RepGuard) significantly improves classification utility and seed-stability over FLTrust under heavy non-IID poisoning, and - under severe heterogeneity or many adversaries - also lowers backdoor ASR substantially (e.g., 0.48 vs FLTrust 0.86 at Dirichlet alpha=0.1); (2) at strong trigger magnitudes no defense reduces backdoor attack success rate (ASR approx 0.95); (3) a controlled trigger-magnitude sweep shows defenses help only for small triggers (ASR 0.10 for RepGuard at magnitude 0.5, vs. 0.40 undefended) and collapse to ASR approx 1.0 by magnitude 2; (4) a triggered-canary check that assumes knowledge of the attacker's trigger - the assumption behind much prior "success" - lowers ASR from 0.49 to 0.12, i.e., trigger knowledge, not representation scoring, suppresses the backdoor; (5) correctly-accounted DP-SGD (varepsilon in [0.3, 16]) costs little utility but does not mitigate the backdoor. I release the protocol so future FL-IDS defenses can be evaluated without the leakage and oracle assumptions that inflate reported robustness.

title: Multi-Token Random-Walk Learning via Meeting-Triggered Information Exchange
abstract: Random walk (RW)-based algorithms are widely used in decentralized learning due to their low communication overhead and scalability. While most existing methods rely on a single token, multiple tokens can explore the network in parallel and exchange information upon meeting. However, the fundamental benefits of such meeting-triggered interactions remain unclear. In this work, we investigate multi-token RW learning under two information exchange policies: \textsc{Average-Gradient} and \textsc{Average-Model}, which average stochastic gradients and updated models, respectively, when tokens meet. We establish iteration complexity lower bounds for non-convex, convex, and strongly convex objectives on complete graphs, which apply to both exchange policies. Compared with single-token RW learning, the scaling factor in these bounds is reduced by a factor of $m^2$ for non-convex and convex objectives, and by an exponentially in $m$ for strongly convex objectives, where $m$ denotes the number of tokens. Numerical experiments reveal distinct behaviors of the two policies under two performance criteria: mean-token loss (the average loss across all tokens) and best-token loss (the minimum loss across all tokens). \textsc{Average-Model} achieves lower mean-token loss and is relatively insensitive to the network-to-token ratio $N/m$, where $N$ is the number of nodes. In contrast, \textsc{Average-Gradient} achieves lower best-token loss but exhibits a trade-off between parallel exploration and gradient interference as $N/m$ decreases.

title: VbotNav-0: Asynchronous Cloud-Edge Dual-Policy Navigation across Indoor and Outdoor Environments
abstract: Continuous indoor-outdoor navigation connects destination-level reasoning with motion decisions that must respond to current observations. We present VbotNav-0, a cloud-edge dual-policy framework that links these processes through asynchronous policy-to-policy conditioning. The cloud policy produces subgoal guidance from visual history, navigation instructions, and route tokens; the edge policy combines available guidance with current RGB and LiDAR observations to generate local trajectories. This formulation allows the local perception-action loop to continue between cloud updates. A common route representation connects indoor paths and outdoor map routes, and the training recipe combines navigation demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded visual question answering (VQA). In the reported closed-loop evaluation of 258 episodes across 145 scenes, VbotNav-0 achieves 55.04% success rate and 55.03% success weighted by path length.

title: Co-adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining for Structured Knowledge Retrieval
abstract: Structured knowledge retrieval acquires task-relevant evidence from structured knowledge sources for downstream tasks. Existing methods rely on unconstrained retrieval or predefined query-rule supervision, such as author-paper rules for scientific discovery and anatomy-drug rules for precision medicine. Such supervision is rarely available in practice. We propose Co-Adaptive Rule Routing and Constraining Retrieval (CoRE), which jointly learns which reasoning rule to assign to each query and how to retrieve evidence under that rule, without predefined query-rule pairs. A routing agent selects a rule, and its corresponding retriever traverses the knowledge base and ranks evidence that satisfies the rule's constraints. Because routing and retrieval are interdependent, CoRE alternates between reinforcement learning for the routing policy and contrastive learning for the rule-constrained retriever. The selected rules provide supervision for retriever training, while retrieval performance rewards the routing policy. This closed-loop process enables both components to co-adapt without explicit query-rule supervision. Experiments on STaRK-QA datasets across scientific discovery, biomedical reasoning, and e-commerce knowledge management demonstrate CoRE's effectiveness. Ablations show the benefit of co-adapting the router and retriever. Generation-based routing transfers across datasets and benefits from multi-domain pretraining followed by target-specific fine-tuning. Analysis of rule usage across queries also informs automatic rule refinement and discovery.

title: E2K: Solving the Entropy Communication Problem
abstract: Entropy has a communication problem. The technical foundations of that problem are documented inEntropy as Infrastructure for Security and Defense (EISD) [1]. This paper does not repeat that work. Itaddresses something different: the gap between what the security community understands and what thepublic can actually talk about. E2K exists to close that gap.Bringing into focus, the problem (E2K), under the problem (Q2K). ⚛️🔎Both sharing the same looming deadline: Q-day. ⏳The public has largely been hearing about Q-day as one problem, Q2K, when there are actually two very difficult problems to contend with: Q2K and E2K.The terms "Entropy2K" and "E2K" are coined by Samantha Lowrimore, October 10, 2026.

title: ClaimArena-LLM: Auditing Adversarial Propagation of False Causal Attributions in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
abstract: Background: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems increasingly rely on structured interaction, debate, and final model-based evaluation, yet an unsupported causal attribution introduced by one participant may propagate through the interaction and influence subsequent decisions. This study introduces ClaimArena-LLM, a controlled framework for auditing adversarial propagation, evidentiary provenance, and final-stage evaluator vulnerability in multi-agent causal reasoning. Methods: ClaimArena-LLM uses 100 synthetic causal incident cases with predefined evidence-supported and false causal propositions. Each case was evaluated under matched adversarial and all-honest debate conditions using four functional roles: investigator, honest analyst, adversarial analyst, and auditor. The experimental program comprised 1460 validated runs, including the 200-run main experiment, claim-source lineage visibility and debate-round ablations, an 800-run balanced model–role rotation, and a 60-run proposition-identifier and presentation-order sensitivity control. Outcomes were scored deterministically from structured causal propositions, evidence references, claim lineage, reports, and auditor verdicts. Results: The adversarial analyst maintained the predefined false causal target with 97.6% mean fidelity. Adversarial exposure increased investigator shifts toward the false target by 16.0 percentage points (Holm-adjusted p = 0.035). At the auditor stage, false-target attribution increased by 11.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.043), verdict contamination by 20.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.002), and semantic provenance validity decreased by 20.0 percentage points (adjusted p = 0.002). Neither the manipulation nor the false target was explicitly detected. The ablations showed no robust adjusted differences, model–role rotation revealed substantial configuration dependence, and no benchmark-characteristic interaction remained significant after Holm correction. The proposition-identifier and presentation-order sensitivity control showed no statistically robust evidence that fixed proposition encoding explained the observed condition contrasts. Conclusions: Adversarial causal influence in multi-agent LLM systems is selective rather than uniformly propagative and depends strongly on functional role and model–role configuration. Within the tested architecture, a final LLM auditor cannot be assumed to provide an independent safeguard against upstream contamination. Reliable evaluation therefore requires separate assessment of causal correctness, propagation, semantic provenance, and final-stage adversarial awareness rather than reliance on final answer accuracy alone.

title: How Does AI-Personalized Marketing Influence Online Purchase Intention? The Roles of Perceived Value, Platform Trust, and Digital Consumer Legal Literacy
abstract: AI-driven personalization has become an important mechanism in interactive digital marketing, yet its influence on consumers’ online purchase intention remains insufficiently understood. Situated within the institutional context of digital platform consumption and personal information protection in China, this study examines 309 consumers who have received formal legal education. Participants were recruited primarily through Chinese universities and professional legal networks. A theoretical model is developed to investigate how perceived AI-personalized recommendations and perceived AI-personalized content influence online purchase intention, with perceived value and platform trust examined as two independent mediating mechanisms and digital consumer legal literacy as a boundary condition. Structural equation modeling (SEM) and artificial neural network (ANN) analysis are jointly employed to provide both explanatory and predictive perspectives. The results show that perceived AI-personalized recommendations and perceived AI-personalized content are both positively associated with online purchase intention and are indirectly related to it through perceived value and platform trust. Digital consumer legal literacy further positively moderates the effects of perceived AI-personalized recommendation and perceived AI-personalized content on perceived value and platform trust, indicating that consumers’ understanding of digital rights, platform responsibilities, and relevant legal rules shapes how they evaluate the value and trustworthiness of algorithmic personalization. The ANN analysis further identifies the relative importance of the predictor variables and provides predictive evidence complementary to the SEM results. By integrating a dual-path mechanism of “utility evaluation–trust evaluation” with digital consumer legal literacy as an institutionally grounded boundary condition, this study advances the theoretical understanding of the relationship between AI-personalized marketing and online purchase intention within the Chinese legal and platform-governance context, while also offering practical implications for optimizing personalized services and strengthening consumer rights governance on digital platforms.

title: Disengaged conversational behaviors and learning in student-AI dialogues for mathematical problem solving
abstract: As the conversational AI agents become integrated into digital learning environments, students’ interaction with these systems can show conversational disengagement, including mocking, misleading, or otherwise diverting the agents. Although task-based disengagement such as gaming the system and off-task actions are well documented, the nature of the consequences of this conversational disengagement in student-AI dialogue remains largely unexplored. This study examined how different types of conversational disengagement relate to middle-school students’ mathematical learning with an AI-powered teachable agent embedded in a large-scale platform. We coded 5,522 utterances from 246 students into six conversational disengagement categories (False Answering, Mocking, Ghosting, Mirroring, Withholding, and Random/Noisy) versus engagement. Regression analyses showed that some disengagements (False Answering and Mocking) were positively associated with post-test scores after controlling for pre-test performance, although these associations did not replicate in a sensitivity analysis restricted to human-annotated utterances. To capture process-level dynamics, we modeled how conversational disengagement ends using a competing-risks approach and separately clustered students based on their turn-by-turn transition probabilities. Most conversational disengagement tended to end within the first few turns, whereas Withholding showed a strong tendency to continue. Students in the highest-performing cluster combined a moderate level of conversational disengagement with strong recovery pathways, whereas the lowest-performing cluster exhibited persistent self-loops without recovery. Together, these findings suggest that some apparent disengagement in conversation with AI may occur within interaction trajectories that subsequently return to productive engagement.

title: HiPAD: A Unified Gait, Audio-Visual, and Personality Fusion Network for Depression Detection, with a Hierarchical Personality Ablation and the Calibration Limits of Domain-Adapted LLMs
abstract: We present HiPAD, a single fusion network submitted to all six sub-tracks of the MPDD-AVG 2026 depression-detection challenge, covering the Elder and Young cohorts and three modality sets (gait, audio-visual, and both), each combined with personality descriptions. The network encodes each available modality with a shared BiLSTM, zero-pads absent modalities, and applies cross-modal attention only when at least two of gait, audio and video are present. Personality, which dominates our results, is kept out of the attention and fused by concatenation. Because the architecture is identical in every sub-track, differences between them reflect the data rather than the model, and we use this to study three questions. Our main finding is that the personality description, roughly 150 tokens about who the subject is, carries more depression signal than audio, video, and gait combined: gait plus personality alone (TLS 0.647) beats every configuration that includes audio and video. First, a four-level ablation of the personality description (L0-L3) quantifies this: removing every personality-derived feature, including the Big Five scores that earlier MPDD ablations keep, lowers the Track-Level Score by 0.499 to 0.507 and leaves the model at chance. Second, domain-adapting the personality encoder with LoRA (7B) or QLoRA (72B) on PHQ-8/9 data raises binary Cohen's $κ$ by 0.13 but lowers the overall score by distorting the PHQ-9 regression; a frozen RoBERTa-large encoder does better at this sample size. Third, at fixed architecture, handcrafted clinical features (eGeMAPS, OpenFace action units) outperform generic deep features (wav2vec2, DenseNet) on the audio-visual tracks. The unified system reaches a cross-track G-Score of 0.482; with under 100 subjects per cohort, the limiting factors are the size of the representation and the calibration of the outputs, not the choice of architecture.

title: PixARG: Pixel-Asynchronous Retrieval-Augmented Diffusion for Fast and Realistic Image Generation
abstract: While diffusion models achieve impressive image generation capabilities, they suffer from high computational costs, implausible artifacts, and limited adaptability to dynamic or private data due to static, centralized training. To address these, we propose PixARG, a novel retrieval-augmented generative framework that integrates dynamic real-world image retrieval into the diffusion pipeline to simultaneously enhance efficiency and visual realism. Specifically, PixARG constructs a pixel-level affinity map between the user's text prompt and the retrieved image to guide a heterogeneous noise initialization. By modulating noise intensity across spatial regions, this mechanism preserves semantically relevant structural priors while perturbing less relevant areas, thereby significantly accelerating convergence. To accommodate this spatially non-uniform noise and ensure synchronized generation, we introduce a pixel-wise asynchronous denoising scheduler and a spatiotemporal denoiser conditioned on the affinity map. Furthermore, we derive an affinity-adaptive training objective that elegantly balances deterministic restoration with stochastic regeneration across pixels. Experiments on LAION and COYO datasets across offline, online, and user-specific settings show PixARG enhances realism and semantic alignment while drastically reducing diffusion steps.

Experiments on LAION and COYO datasets across offline, online, and user-specific settings show PixARG enhances realism and semantic alignment while drastically reducing diffusion steps.

title: Evaluating Bias in Chinese Large Language Models across Tasks and Registers: Task Operationalization Effects and Irony Classification Risks
abstract: In Chinese content governance, large language models are increasingly used to identify toxic and discriminatory expressions, yet both task operationalization and ironic expression can alter bias measurement readings. We conducted a preregistered multi-task behavioral audit of multiple Chinese large language models. In the content classification experiment, the core panel's classification error rate rose from 10.9% in the formal register to 23.5% in the yinyang (an echoic-irony register) version, a risk difference of +12.7 percentage points. (95% CI [+9.7, +15.7]). Inter-rater agreement was lower in the yinyang register (majority-vote kappa = 0.299), so the increase contains a component of label uncertainty propagation, but the direction of increase was consistent under both adjudicated and majority-vote reference standards. Explicit irony-aware prompts reduced the intervention panel's error rate by 9.6 percentage points. We operationalized the 29 shared proposition anchors into three task forms: social consensus estimation (Form A), high-stakes decision (Form B), and controlled association rating (Form C); independent manipulation checks found that all 58 A-C comparison units received unanimous agreement, whereas the low A-B convergence was confirmed by calibrated majority adjudication (87.8% supporting the minority judgment); on the irony-probe materials, the interactions of B and C relative to A were +0.577 and +1.121, respectively. Thus, when evaluating large language models for Chinese content governance, the effect of task operationalization on bias readings is an empirical question that requires data to answer, and safety evaluation should incorporate the ironic register as a test condition.

title: Quantum-Fisher-information-aware optimization yields a quantum reservoir advantage over tuned classical reservoirs
abstract: We show that a quantum reservoir computer optimized with its quantum Fisher information (QFI) has a quantum advantage over a classical reservoir of equal readout cost, provided by a quantum-information advantage: optimizing the quantum parameters with the QFI metric. On Mackey-Glass forecasting, a driven Jaynes-Cummings reservoir with one to three atoms beats a tuned echo-state network at every size from 4 to 30 trained weights, by 25-69% in held-out error, and is ahead of 99.5% of 10,000 random networks. After grid and Bayesian searches saturate, the QFI-aware stage lowers the error by 29-51% at 12-30 weights, beyond equal-budget black-box search or classical-parameter gradients alone, and at 30 weights turns a loss into a win. We then derive a fundamental QFI bound on the first-order rate of change of the retrained loss and factorize the gap to this bound into five link efficiencies that identify the physical mechanism limiting optimization.

title: Scaffold or Cognitive Crutch? A Two-Level Meta-Analysis of AI Scaffolding Effects on Achievement and Self-Regulated Learning in STEM Education
abstract: Background. Artificial intelligence (AI) now mediates much of science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning, yet adoption has outpaced theory. The tension is whether AI scaffolding relieves cognitive burden or performs the self-regulatory work autonomy requires, and implementation varies too widely for a single average to describe. Objectives. This review estimates the pooled effect of AI scaffolding on STEM achievement and self-regulated learning, tests whether technological paradigm moderates that effect, and asks whether the literature can evaluate learning after support is withdrawn. Methods. Under PRISMA 2020, four platforms searched in October 2026 (spanning 2021–2026) yielded 21,819 records; 13,786 unique records were dual-screened into an 83-record corpus, then 41 extracted cohorts. Each contributes one harmonised contrast (k = 29; N = 3,709), so within-study dependence is structurally absent. Effects were pooled by two-level random-effects meta-analysis fitted with restricted maximum likelihood and Knapp–Hartung adjustment. Results. The pooled effect was Hedges g = 0.8045 (95% CI [0.5469, 1.0621]), with τ² = 0.4410 and I² = 92.78%. The 95% prediction interval [−0.5846, 2.1936] spans zero, and no moderator reached significance. Notably, 27 of 29 cohorts (93.1%) never withdrew support, and none measured unassisted performance after removal. Conclusions. AI scaffolding yields a large but implementation-dependent gain, consistent with extraneous-load offloading rather than cognitive substitution. The decisive finding is the shape of the evidence base: the field measured a human-AI system in assembly and stayed silent on the competence of the human alone. We name this evidentiary void the Autonomy Gap. Keywords: artificial intelligence; self-regulated learning; STEM education; scaffolding fading; cognitive load theory; transfer of responsibility; meta-analysis; evidence synthesis

title: Hybrid Vector–Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Resource Planning: Contextual Grounding, Referential Integrity, and Hallucination Mitigation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become the default mechanism for grounding large language models (LLMs) in private corpora, yet the dominant implementation, dense vector similarity over flat text chunks, is a poor structural match for enterprise resource planning (ERP) data. ERP records are not prose: they are normalised, heavily cross-referenced, temporally versioned tuples whose meaning derives from join paths (purchase requisition → purchase order → goods receipt → supplier invoice → payment) rather than from lexical or semantic proximity. A retriever that scores chunks independently by cosine similarity has no mechanism for guaranteeing that the documents it returns are mutually consistent or that they refer to the same business object, and the resulting evidence sets invite a characteristic failure mode we term referential hallucination: fluent output that correctly cites individual documents but silently fabricates the relationships between them. This paper proposes HVG-RAG, a hybrid vector–graph retrieval architecture for ERP question answering, and makes three contributions. First, we formalise referential integrity as a first-class retrieval-time constraint rather than a post-hoc evaluation criterion, and specify a constraint-satisfaction verifier that operates over an ontology-bound property graph induced from ERP metadata. Second, we introduce an adaptive fusion policy in which the weight assigned to vector versus graph evidence is predicted per query from an estimated reasoning depth, rather than fixed by a global hyperparameter. Third, we attach bitemporal validity intervals to graph edges so that “as-of” queries, pervasive in finance and audit, are answered against the state of record at the relevant time rather than against current master data. We develop the accompanying mathematics, give complexity bounds, and specify a reproducible evaluation protocol with ERP-specific metrics. We evaluate the framework on ERP-Bench-P2P, an executable procure-to-pay benchmark released with this paper: 19,632 documents projected from a normalised schema, a 47,914-edge foreign-key graph, and 1,700 questions stratified by reasoning depth with gold provenance. The results reported here are measured on that benchmark rather than simulated. At a retrieval budget of 100 documents, hybrid dense-sparse retrieval answers 100% of one-hop questions and 0.6% of two-hop questions, because the documents joined by a foreign key share almost no vocabulary; HVG-RAG answers 100%, 91.5%, 99.1% and 97.9% of one- to four-hop questions at a measured p95 latency of 96 ms. Two findings run against our own expectations and we report them as such: five-hop questions requiring selection of the contract revision effective at the transaction date remain largely unsolved (57.1% at k = 100, 0.3% at k = 20), and a graph-only retriever is competitive with the proposed system whenever the query names an identifier, its advantage disappearing only when the anchor entity must first be located by description. End-to-end generation quality is not measured here and remains future work.

title: Rate-Based Causal Discovery for Heavy-Tailed Models
abstract: In many complex systems, such as river networks and financial markets, extreme events propagate from causes to their effects, and the largest observations carry the most information about the underlying causal structure. Existing methods for causal discovery in extremes, however, are tailored to specific mechanisms, such as linear or max-linear models. This work develops causal discovery for heavy-tailed homogeneous structural causal models, a flexible class that contains linear, max-linear and norm-type mechanisms, which may differ from node to node. In these models, the causal structure is encoded by ancestral impulse responses, which measure how a shock at one node is transmitted to its descendants. We propose the extremal minimum ratio estimator of these responses, which uses only observations in which the potential cause is extreme. The estimator is consistent under regular variation alone, and we derive its exact rates of convergence and limiting distributions, which depend on both the causal relation and the type of mechanism. Building on these rates, we construct consistent estimators of the causal order and of the full set of ancestral relations, using a threshold that adapts to the data and requires no knowledge of the tail index. The method is illustrated on simulated data and on river discharges in the upper Danube basin.

title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
abstract: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin Gödel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.

title: SXEAI(Sextic Equation AI)
abstract: ---license: mit--- # SXEAI: Reverse-Engineering the Mathematics Learned by a Neural Sextic Solver ## Abstract Can a neural network learn not only to solve an algebraic problem, but also to develop an internal mathematical representation of the problem that we can reverse-engineer? This is the main question behind **SXEAI**, an experimental project focused on neural networks that recover the six roots of a general polynomial of degree six from its coefficients. The objective is deliberately different from a conventional machine-learning benchmark. We are not primarily interested in obtaining the smallest possible root prediction error. Instead, we want to understand **what the network computes internally**. Across a sequence of experiments, SXEAI repeatedly developed hidden representations that could be approximated by compact combinations of symmetric polynomial quantities, power sums, centered moments, depressed-polynomial coefficients, and related algebraic features. Some of these internal coordinates could be discovered blindly, reproduced on unseen data, and even replaced causally by their symbolic approximations without substantially changing downstream network behavior. The resulting picture is not yet a discovered closed-form solution of the general sextic equation. It is something more precise and, in our view, more interesting: evidence that a neural algebraic solver can spontaneously organize its hidden state into a structured mathematical coordinate system that can be partially reconstructed and experimentally manipulated. --- # 1. The question behind SXEAI A standard neural network experiment asks a simple question: > Can the network learn the mapping from inputs to outputs? For a sextic polynomial, $$P(z)=z^6+p_5z^5+p_4z^4+p_3z^3+p_2z^2+p_1z+p_0,$$ the conventional task would be: $$(p_5,p_4,p_3,p_2,p_1,p_0)\longrightarrow(r_1,\ldots,r_6),$$ where $$P(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{6}(z-r_i).$$ One can then measure MAE, RMSE, maximum root error, or polynomial reconstruction error. SXEAI asks a different question: $$\boxed{\text{What mathematical representation does the network build internally?}}$$ The network may not need to directly represent each root at every stage. It could instead construct intermediate quantities such as $$-\frac{p_5}{6},$$ power sums $$s_k=\sum_i r_i^k,$$ centered moments $$q_k=\frac16\sum_i(r_i-\mu)^k,$$ or more complicated combinations such as $$s_2s_3,\qquad s_2s_4,\qquad q_3q_4.$$ The central idea of the project is therefore to treat the network itself as a mathematical object that can be reverse-engineered. --- # 2. Why the sextic problem? The sextic is an interesting test case because it is already beyond the regime where one should expect a simple universal elementary formula for the roots. For low-degree equations, classical symbolic methods provide familiar closed forms. At degree six, the algebraic structure becomes substantially richer. This makes the sextic a useful environment for asking: > Does a neural solver rediscover recognizable algebraic coordinates, or does it develop a completely different internal representation? We do not assume in advance that the answer must involve radicals. That distinction became increasingly important as the project progressed. --- # 3. The model SXEAI uses a custom layer called `SexticLayer`. A layer first computes $$z=Wx+b,$$ then applies a trainable sixth-degree polynomial $$Az^6+Bz^5+Cz^4+Dz^3+Ez^2+Fz+G,$$ followed by normalization and GELU. The polynomial activation is initialized close to a quadratic form, so the network starts from a relatively simple nonlinear regime but can learn higher-order behavior. The main complex model used in the later experiments has approximately 1.2 million parameters and consists of 24 such layers with hidden width 223. The final network maps a 12-dimensional real representation of the polynomial coefficients to 12 real values representing six complex roots: $$[\Re r_1,\Im r_1,\ldots,\Re r_6,\Im r_6].$$ This architecture is intentionally unusual. Rather than hiding all nonlinearity inside a standard ReLU or GELU network, we give the model explicit trainable polynomial operations and then ask what mathematical structure emerges. --- # 4. Data generation The polynomial is generated from its roots. For six roots $$r_1,\ldots,r_6,$$ we construct $$P(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{6}(z-r_i).$$ The network does not receive the roots. It receives only the resulting coefficients. For the complex experiments, roots are represented by real and imaginary parts: $$r_i=a_i+ib_i.$$ The root generation, normalization, coefficient construction, ordering and scaling are kept fixed across the main comparisons. The training protocol used in the main experiments includes: * 350,000 training samples;* batch size 768;* 125 epochs;* AdamW;* learning rate \(3\times10^{-4}\);* weight decay \(10^{-4}\);* gradient clipping at 1.0;* SmoothL1 loss. The dataset mixes real, natural/integer-like and fully complex root configurations. --- # 5. The first discovery: the network finds the center One of the earliest and most persistent observations was the appearance of $$\boxed{\mu=-\frac{p_5}{6}}.$$ Since $$p_5=-\sum_i r_i,$$ we have $$\mu=\frac16\sum_i r_i.$$ In other words, the first layers repeatedly discovered the **mean of the roots**. This was not a one-off correlation. Across different architectures and training runs, early hidden units consistently exhibited strong alignment with this quantity. That suggested an important possibility: > the network may first transform the problem into a coordinate system centered around the roots before attempting to recover their detailed structure. --- # 6. From coefficients to symmetric quantities The next step was to search hidden activations against a library of algebraically meaningful quantities. Among the most important were the power sums $$s_k=\sum_i r_i^k,$$ together with centered moments $$q_k=\frac16\sum_i(r_i-\mu)^k$$ and the coefficients of the depressed sextic obtained after translating the variable by the root mean. Newton identities provide the connection between these representations. For example, $$s_1=\sum_i r_i=-p_5,$$ and $$s_2,\;s_3,\ldots$$ can be expressed recursively in terms of the polynomial coefficients. This means the network has access, through ordinary algebraic transformations, to several equivalent coordinate systems describing the same root configuration. The symbolic experiments suggested that it was not merely using raw coefficient coordinates. It repeatedly rediscovered combinations of the more natural symmetric quantities. --- # 7. Deep layers developed richer combinations In deeper networks we began to find hidden units whose activations could be approximated by combinations such as $$a s_3+b s_5+c\,s_2s_3,$$ or $$a s_6+b\,s_2s_4+c\,q_4.$$ Examples from earlier high-performing real-root models included expressions such as $$1.7637s_3+0.2457s_5-1.2059s_2s_3$$ with \(R^2\) around 0.80, and $$-0.7720s_1-0.7597s_3+0.6254s_2s_3$$ with \(R^2\) around 0.89.
