title: From Risk-Sensitive Foraging to Scalable Portfolio Rebalancing: State-Conditioned Artificial Bee Colony Optimization of Cost-Aware Omega
abstract: This study examines whether candidate-level gain–loss information improves search for cost-aware portfolio rebalancing. We propose Risk-Sensitive Foraging Artificial Bee Colony (RSF-ABC) for long-only portfolios with exact cardinality and active-weight bounds. A bounded state derived from the Omega objective controls the probability of heavy-tailed exploration versus conservative best-guided search. A state-independent mixture of the same operators isolates the value of state conditioning. Monthly evaluation on U.S. industry portfolios uses 504-day formation windows and proportional transaction costs. Mean net Omega is 1.1635 for RSF-ABC, 1.1284 for Standard ABC, 1.1342 for Fixed-Mix-ABC, 1.1410 for particle swarm optimization, and 1.1450 for differential evolution. Monthly turnover is 0.4780 versus 0.5570 for Standard ABC. The proposed method leads in five of seven boundary conditions; deterministic alternatives lead in two. At 49 assets, its reported median runtime is 1.11 s versus 1.08 s for Standard ABC. These results support the evaluated state–operator coupling.

title: Text-Guided Medical Image Segmentation via Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations
abstract: Specifying segmentation targets with natural language provides flexible semantic conditioning for medical image segmentation. However, existing methods still struggle to reliably ground high-level textual semantics into accurate pixel-level spatial prompts, especially under low-contrast lesions, ambiguous boundaries, and visually similar anatomical contexts. In this paper, we propose RADAR (Residual Aggregation and Dense Alignment Representations), a parameter-efficient framework for text-guided medical image segmentation. RADAR explicitly decouples and synergizes the medical semantic anchoring capability of BiomedCLIP with the prompt-driven mask decoding ability of MedSAM2, while enabling low-cost task adaptation via LoRA. Specifically, Guided Residual Depth Aggregation adaptively aggregates cross-layer features under semantic guidance to alleviate delayed textual injection and deep semantic dilution. Structured Dense Representation Alignment leverages a frozen BiomedCLIP to construct crop-level target, boundary, and context anchors, improving the local discriminability of dense features and the reliability of automatic prompts. Multi-modal Prompt Generation further converts cross-modal semantic responses into composite text, point, and mask prompts for MedSAM2 decoding. Experiments on three public medical image segmentation datasets show that RADAR achieves competitive performance with only 0.74M trainable parameters, demonstrating its effectiveness in parameter-efficient adaptation, semantic grounding, and dense representation enhancement. The source code is available at https://github.com/JGuiidev/RADAR.

title: Protecting Shared Agent Workflows from Invalidation Attacks with Signed Trajectories and Runtime Verification
abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents increasingly rely on shared workflow repositories to transfer experience across tasks and agents. By abstracting past executions into reusable workflow graphs, such systems significantly improve planning efficiency and generalization. However, this emerging paradigm introduces a new and underexplored security risk: if the shared repository is compromised, tampered workflows can systematically mislead downstream agents, inducing persistent execution failures or unsafe behaviors. In this work, we present a principled protection framework for shared agent workflows based on signed trajectories and runtime verification. We require all cloud-collected trajectories used for workflow generation to be cryptographically signed, with each trajectory representing a concrete execution instance. Prior to repository inclusion, trajectories undergo a unified screening process to ensure correctness and validity. When an agent retrieves a workflow from the shared repository, it also obtains a small set of signed supporting trajectories and verifies both their cryptographic integrity and their semantic consistency with the workflow. To make this practical for branching workflows, we further propose a runtime, path-aware retrieval strategy that dynamically fetches only the signed trajectories relevant to the execution path actually taken by the agent, substantially reducing communication and verification overhead. Extensive experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks show that workflow invalidation attacks achieve up to 90.12% success rates, degrading agent inference performance by up to 73.16 percentage points in accuracy without effective workflow protection. In addition, the proposed protection achieves an average F1 score of 85.26% and a detection rate of 79.97%, outperforming existing baselines by about 2.02x.

title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.

title: Equi-rank preservation and branching in finite intuitionistic Kripke models
abstract: 抄録 We study existential-positive definability under forward homomorphisms of finite rooted intuitionistic Kripke models with expanding domains. For a nonempty class of frames of height at most two, let the allowed leaf counts form a set of nonnegative integers. With no background theory and a finite relational signature containing a relation symbol, preservation admits an existential-positive definition of no greater quantifier rank precisely when only the singleton frame is allowed or some admitted frame has at least two leaves. Uniformly over all finite relational signatures and all background theories forbidding finite positive atomic patterns, the corresponding condition is that only the singleton is allowed or the leaf counts are unbounded. Every bounded class admitting a nonsingleton frame has a finite background theory and a rank-one preserved sentence with no existential-positive root equivalent. The counterexample combines mutually incompatible unary labels with the antecedent of a known bounded-branching axiom. A modular transfer theorem separates compatibility of finite background diagrams, a classical quantitative preservation input, and availability of branching targets. On unrestricted finite rooted frames, designated-signature equi-rank preservation extends to possibly infinite background theories of this form. Examples separate this extension from finite-subtheory reductions and demonstrate the failure of an input-rank bound for general coherent backgrounds. Restricted-frame equivalence is asserted at roots. AI利用の開示 OpenAI Codex assisted with manuscript inventory, bibliographic extraction and preparation of this deposit. title: What to Reuse in Generative Robot Policies? A Solver-Aware Mathematical Analysis of Training-Free Output Caching for Action Generation
abstract: Diffusion- and flow-matching-based generative robot policies, including recent vision–language–action (VLA) models, generate continuous action chunks by repeatedly invoking an action generator over multiple generation steps, which constitutes a major bottleneck for real-time robot control. Training-free output caching—recomputing the generator only at selected steps and reusing its output in between—is an attractive remedy, but its mathematical properties and stability criteria have not been rigorously examined for robot action generation. This paper provides a solver-aware mathematical analysis of what quantity should be reused. We first prove a numerical degeneracy result: for explicit Euler integrators applied to deterministic linear flow-matching heads, blockwise velocity output reuse is exactly equivalent to coarse-grid Euler integration, and hence to native few-step inference; output caching in this regime is a reparameterization of step reduction rather than a distinct numerical algorithm. In contrast, for stochastic ancestral samplers, the equivalence fails and the choice of reuse space becomes mathematically decisive. We prove that the staleness error of a cached noise estimate is amplified into endpoint (clean-action) error by the inverse root signal-to-noise ratio SNR(τ)−1/2=στ/ατ, which diverges at high-noise steps (τ→0), whereas caching the posterior-mean endpoint propagates staleness non-expansively: an exact error recursion shows that the cumulative deviation of the generated action is uniformly bounded by the largest staleness error under endpoint-space caching, while under noise-space caching the recursion is expansive and staleness incurred at high-noise steps is transferred to the final action with unbounded gain. A Tweedie-type sensitivity identity further establishes that the spectral norm of the endpoint Jacobian is directly controlled by the conditional posterior covariance of actions given observation conditioning, explaining why endpoints form a mathematically stable target when conditioned on dense observations. The theoretical framework is instantiated as EndCache, a training-free endpoint-space caching protocol, and validated empirically without any policy retraining: in a controlled study over ∼60 Diffusion Policy checkpoints, endpoint-space caching preserves task success (85.9% vs. an 87.2% baseline) while noise-space caching collapses to 12.2%—a 73.7 percentage-point performance gap predicted by our amplification analysis; iso-budget numerical evaluations on two flow-matching VLA models confirm the degeneracy proposition to within 0.5 percentage points; and across diffusion/flow-matching policies and robotic simulation benchmarks, endpoint-space reuse reduces action-generator calls with up to 2.7× end-to-end speedup while keeping task success near baseline.

title: (Implicitly) Characterizing Probabilistic Polynomial Time as Used in Cryptography
abstract: In this paper, we show how a recently introduced $λ$-calculus for randomized computation, called $λ\mathbf{BLL}$, can accurately capture the notions of first- and second-order polytime computations used in cryptographic definitions and proofs. These results, spelled out in the style of so-called \emph{implicit computational complexity}, imply that $λ\mathbf{BLL}$ is sufficiently powerful to express experiments and adversaries as used in cryptography, and that reductions, when formulated within the calculus, are guaranteed to be complexity-preserving. Remarkably, while polynomial-time soundness holds for the full calculus, polynomial-time completeness already follows in presence of a minimal finite set of basic functions.

title: Understanding Hidden Spatial Preferences in Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Bayesian optimization uses posterior uncertainty to decide where to explore, but this uncertainty is not spatially neutral. On bounded domains, Gaussian-process posterior variance is typically larger near faces, edges, and corners, giving variance-based acquisition functions a systematic boundary bias. This spatial preference is usually inherited from the surrogate rather than chosen as part of the exploration strategy. We separate these roles by keeping the predictive model fixed and modifying the spatial preference of the exploration term. We control the preference with spatial weight fields and amortize their construction with neural surrogates. Controlled experiments show that the Gaussian process' default boundary bias changes which parts of the domain are explored and which optima are reached. We compare three alternative exploration principles and find, across standard benchmark functions and stochastic robot-pushing tasks, that they can often lower regret, particularly early in the optimization. The spatial structure of posterior uncertainty is therefore not a neutral default: it shapes the exploration strategy and can materially affect optimization performance.

title: Validation of diagnostic artificial intelligence models for prostate pathology in a Middle Eastern cohort
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) for pathology is accelerating cancer diagnostics. For global adoption, studies in currently under-represented populations - where the potential gains from AI may also be greatest - are needed. We present the first external validation study in a Middle Eastern setting, focusing on diagnosis and Gleason grading of prostate cancer. We digitised 339 prostate glass slides from Kurdistan, Iraq, representing a consecutive series of 185 patients from 2013 to 2024. Each slide was scanned on three digital pathology scanners, generating 1,017 whole-slide images. title: Token-Generation-Control-Deterministic-Logical-Timeline
abstract: Text generation by large language models is essentially a probabilistic sampling process: the model computes a probability distribution over the next token based on the input context, and then samples a token from that distribution. This probabilistic design gives large models creativity but also introduces a fundamental engineering problem: the same input may produce different outputs at different times, in different environments, or on different hardware. For AI agents (automated trading, code generation, industrial control) that require stability and reproducibility, this non-determinism is fatal. This paper proposes a token generation control method based on a deterministic logical timeline. The method uses the logical state S(n) output by a Protocol Security State Machine (PSSM) as the initialization seed of a pseudo-random number generator (PRNG), replacing random sources based on physical time or hardware noise, thereby transforming the token sampling process from "physical non-determinism" to "logical determinism". The paper provides the complete token generation flow, two working modes (deterministic mode and divergent-but-reproducible mode), a cryptographically bound record format, and, building on the independent verification and replay mechanism disclosed in the applicant's prior patent, an auditing method for token generation records. The method does not change the model's native probability distribution (intelligence representation); it only controls the token sampling path, achieving cryptographic-level determinism across environments, hardware, and frameworks.

title: Multi-Agent Path Planning Based on Coulomb’s Law and PER-MADDPG
abstract: Multi-agent path planning remains a challenging problem in deep reinforcement learning due to inefficient coordination, excessive exploration, and unstable training dynamics. Although Multi-Agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (MADDPG) has been widely adopted for cooperative decision-making tasks, its performance is often limited by poor sample efficiency and insufficient coordination in complex environments. To address these issues, this paper proposes a physics-guided multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that integrates a Coulomb’s law-inspired interaction mechanism with prioritized experience replay (PER). A virtual potential field based on Coulomb-like repulsive forces is introduced to provide structured action guidance, thereby reducing ineffective exploration and improving inter-agent coordination. In addition, PER is incorporated into MADDPG to enhance sample utilization and stabilize policy learning. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently achieves better task performance and path planning efficiency than baseline approaches across multiple scenarios. The results validate the effectiveness of integrating physical interaction priors into multi-agent reinforcement learning for complex path planning tasks.

title: Modeling Cooperation as Information Flow: Ripple Structures and Behavioral Digital Twins
abstract: Recent advances in articial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models, havesignicantly improved performance in language understanding, vision, and reasoning. How-ever, a fundamental limitation remains: current AI systems still lack an explicit under-standing of the logical structure by which humans make decisions within specic situationsand relationships. This limitation is not merely a shortage of intelligence, but a missinglayer of context-dependent decision logic. This study proposes a theoretical framework andmethodological protocol that redenes human cooperation as an observable information owrather than a psychological or moral phenomenon. We model cooperative propagation asRipple structures, which are directional causal chains of actions in which A helps B and B inturn helps C, and we introduce the concept of a Behavioral Digital Twin, dened as a map-ping of decision logic derived from situation, relationships, and action history. We furtherpresent a non-interventional observational protocol for capturing naturally occurring coop-erative behaviors through naturalistic observation environments, and outline a validationframework for future empirical work. All behavioral events remain voluntary; the proto-col introduces observation infrastructure without prescribing or incentivizing actions. Allgures and examples in this manuscript are conceptual illustrations intended to clarify the-oretical constructs. This work aims to provide a foundational layer connecting AI research,social systems research, and Web3 governance.

title: A Covariance-Guided Pursuit Birds of Prey-Based Optimization for global optimization and UAV path planning
abstract: Birds of Prey-Based Optimization (BPBO) may suffer from insufficient directional guidance, undifferentiated population learning, and premature stagnation when solving rotated, multimodal, and high-dimensional optimization problems. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Covariance-Guided Pursuit Birds of Prey-Based Optimization (CGP-BPBO) algorithm integrating three complementary mechanisms. Elite Memory Covariance Rotation Guidance (EMCRG) uses the covariance structure of elite individuals to introduce anisotropic correction into the best-guided branch. Rank-Based Dynamic Pursuit Learning (RBDPL) assigns different learning behaviors according to individual fitness ranks. Stagnation-Aware Gaussian-Cauchy Mutation (SAGCM) applies state-dependent perturbations to restore diversity when search improvement ceases. CGP-BPBO was evaluated using the IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation 2017 (CEC2017) and 2022 (CEC2022) benchmark suites under 30 independent runs. After excluding the officially deprecated CEC2017 F2 function, CGP-BPBO achieved the best mean result on 17 of the remaining 29 CEC2017 functions and outperformed the original BPBO on all 29 functions in terms of the reported mean values. On the 10- and 20-dimensional CEC2022 suites, it outperformed BPBO on 12 of 12 and 11 of 12 functions, respectively. Based on the mean results reported in the benchmark tables, CGP-BPBO obtained the lowest Friedman mean ranks of 1.79, 1.79, and 2.96 for CEC2017-30D, CEC2022-10D, and CEC2022-20D, respectively. In the three-dimensional unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) path-planning experiment, CGP-BPBO achieved a mean path cost of 239.8048 and a standard deviation of 26.2686, representing reductions of 21.74% and 59.68%, respectively, compared with BPBO. These results demonstrate the competitiveness of CGP-BPBO in numerical optimization and constrained path planning, while its covariance decomposition introduces additional computational cost in high-dimensional problems.

title: Game-Theoretic Reinforcement Learning based Topology-Agnostic Defense for Virtual Power Plants
abstract: The rapid proliferation of distributed energy resources (DERs) aggregated by virtual power plants (VPPs) elevates cybersecurity risk by expanding the attack surface. A coordinated cyberattack has the potential to disrupt distribution-system, bulk-system, and market operations. Existing cyberphysical defense strategies largely assume access to grid network models and operating conditions, which may not be available to third-party aggregators. This paper proposes a novel hybrid, perturbation-based cyber-physical defense for VPP-operated DERs that blends game-theoretic planning with model-free reinforcement learning (RL) under a Bayesian belief-update framework. Topology agnosticism is defined from the VPP information and implementation perspective: the VPP does not require access to the feeder topology, line parameters, switching configuration, or full system state. This work advances the state of the art through three contributions: (1) a multi-output Gaussian process with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for discrete attacker-type inference, probability of detection, and confidence of detection for modeling the belief distribution; (2) moment-matched Gaussian propagation of posterior beliefs across episodes; and (3) an RL policy that adaptively integrates Stackelberg leader (VPP) actions with exploration. Furthermore, we establish equilibrium existence and derive an episode-level closed-loop utility bound connecting attacker-belief uncertainty with GT-RL action alignment. Evaluations on IEEE 13- and 123-Bus feeders with DER portfolios demonstrate effective detection under attacker-model uncertainty and evaluated feeder re-configuration conditions, while requiring no explicit feeder-topology knowledge. Overall, the results indicate that combining bi-level game-theoretic planning, nonparametric Bayesian inference, and adaptive RL is a promising direction for VPP cybersecurity.

title: Duality Theory for Filter Stability in Hidden Markov Models
abstract: This article is concerned with the problem of nonlinear (stochastic) filter stability for a discrete time hidden Markov model (HMM) with finite state and observation spaces. For this purpose, a comprehensive duality theory is developed whereby the dual control system is a backward stochastic difference equation (BSDE). The duality is expressed in two inter-related forms. In its variational form, the minimum mean squared error of optimal filtering equals the value of a dual optimal control problem. In its structural form, controllability (resp. stabilizability) of the BSDE and observability (resp. detectability) of the HMM are dual properties. The dual optimal control problem supplies the Lyapunov function and the dissipation: the former is the value function (a variance), the latter the optimal running cost accumulated over the horizon. The main result is an invariance principle: under any one of three model properties---ergodicity of the Markov matrix, or observability or detectability of the HMM---zero dissipation over a finite horizon forces the Lyapunov function to vanish. A converse is also obtained: detectability is necessary. Two applications are given. The first is filter stability in chi-squared divergence: the invariance principle is applied in the manner of LaSalle, to limits of trajectories along which the dissipation vanishes asymptotically, the role of the model properties being to render the zero-dissipation set trivial. The second is a quantitative form of the invariance principle, through a Poincare constant, from which convergence rates follow. Both the model properties that govern stability and the Lyapunov function that certifies it are thus obtained from a dual optimal control problem, as in the classical theory for the linear Gaussian model.

title: Elektron tijoratda sun'iy intellektdan foydalanishning kichik biznes savdo hajmiga ta'siri
abstract: Ushbu maqolada sun'iy intellekt (AI) dan foydalanishning kichik biznes elektron tijoratida savdo ko'rsatkichlari va iqtisodiy samaradorlikka ta'siri o'rganiladi. O'zbekistonning 2023-2025 yillardagi rasmiy elektron tijorat statistikasi, xalqaro eksperimental dalillar va o'zbek tadqiqotchilarining tadqiqotlariga tayanib, ushbu maqolada AI asosidagi tavsiya tizimlari, aqlli chatbotlar, talabni prognozlash va marketingni avtomatlashtirish onlayn savdoga qanday ta'sir qilishining iqtisodiy mexanizmlari o'rganiladi. Tadqiqot natijalari shuni ko'rsatadiki, AI axborot assimetriyasini kamaytirish va mijozlar bilan aloqani kuchaytirish orqali savdo ko'rsatkichlarini yaxshilashi mumkin. Biroq, iqtisodiy foyda ma'lumotlar sifati, amalga oshirish xarajatlari va boshqaruv imkoniyatlariga bog'liq. Maqolada O'zbekistondagi kichik elektron tijorat korxonalari tomonidan AI texnologiyalarini barqaror joriy etish bo'yicha amaliy tavsiyalar berilgan.

title: Word-Aligned Prosody Reflects Speaker Differences More Than Depression or PTSD Severity
abstract: Word-aligned prosody is increasingly used to detect depression and posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), yet the stability and clinical relevance of these measurements remain unclear. We examine stability at two levels. At the word level, we ask whether a speaker produces the same word in a similar speaker-specific way across different utterance contexts. At the speaker level, we ask whether averaging prosody across many words produces consistent speaker scores across separate recordings. Drawing on principles of psychological measurement, we compare these representations in four corpora spanning acted, spontaneous, and clinical speech. Word-specific deviations show little cross-context recurrence (0.01-0.16), whereas speaker summaries are highly consistent, reaching 0.997 in ESD, 0.73-0.90 in MSP-Podcast, and 0.84-0.996 in DAIC-WOZ and PTSD-STOP. Despite this consistency, associations with depression or PTSD severity do not exceed 0.15; equivalence tests exclude effects of 0.30 in all analyses and 0.20 in DAIC-WOZ, while within-person associations with daily PTSD symptoms are near zero ($|ρ|\leq0.04$). Thus, aggregation yields stable speaker-level prosodic measures, but these measures do not detectably track depression or PTSD severity in the studied corpora. Code is available at https://github.com/jen900704/word-aligned-prosody.

title: Predict in Chunks, Revise in Spans: History-conditioned Action Regeneration for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Action chunking improves temporal coherence in visuomotor imitation learning by jointly predicting sequences of future actions. However, many existing policies regenerate entire action chunks even when errors are localized, potentially replacing otherwise valid predictions. We introduce Contextual Masked Action Policy (CMAP), a visuomotor policy that refines continuous action chunks through history-conditioned local regeneration. Specifically, CMAP introduces a history-conditioned action tape that combines executed commands with masked future positions to produce coarse action predictions and per-step uncertainty scores. An uncertainty-guided span regeneration mechanism then selects a high-uncertainty contiguous span and reconstructs it using the executed history and retained future predictions as context. By jointly reconstructing neighboring actions, CMAP models local temporal dependencies while preserving all predictions outside the selected span. Extensive experiments on nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that CMAP achieves superior overall performance over several competitive baselines. Ablation studies validate the complementary contributions of its key components, while held-out trajectory analysis shows that local regeneration reduces prediction errors within selected spans.

title: AcrossVAM2.0: Conflict-Aware Point Supervision for Parameter-Efficient Video Diffusion Adaptation
abstract: Explicit point correspondence is attractive for adapting video generators: it describes how visible surfaces move, but can overwrite the appearance prior learned by a large pretrained model. We study this tension in a 5.01B-parameter text-to-video diffusion transformer. ACROSSVAM2.0 combines a confidence-weighted track-and-visibility head, zero-initialized residual feedback, and asymmetric PCGrad that removes only the auxiliary component opposing the primary flow-matching gradient on shared LoRA parameters. The design preserves the generator exactly at initialization and protects its primary update during adaptation. In a four-way ablation trained for 1,000 steps with three independent seeds, the full method lowers KLT forward-backward cycle error in all three seeds relative to a matched flow-only continuation (mean seed-level difference -0.00711, SD 0.00505), while robust sharpness remains positive in all three. An expanded 24-prompt evaluation (216 videos) yields 9.7% lower aggregate CoTracker3 cycle error than the matched control and near-matched performance on six VBench dimensions; however, the seed-level tracking effect is heterogeneous and I3D-FVD regresses from 0.1824 to 0.2022. These results support a bounded claim: conflict-aware adaptation improves correspondence consistency without broad perceptual degradation, but does not uniformly improve video quality. We release equations, pseudocode, matched outputs, source tables, and artifact provenance.

title: Characterization and forecasting of national-scale solar power ramp events
abstract: The rapid growth of solar energy is reshaping power system operations and increasing the complexity of grid management. As photovoltaic (PV) capacity expands, short-term fluctuations in PV generation introduce substantial operational uncertainty. At the same time, solar power ramp events intensify risks of grid instability and unplanned outages due to sudden large power fluctuations. Accurate identification, forecasting and mitigation of solar ramp events are therefore critical to maintaining grid stability. In this study, we characterize national-scale solar PV ramp events based on two years of PV power production from 6434 PV stations at 15-minute resolution. We develop quantitative metrics to define solar ramp events and systematically characterize their occurrence, frequency, and magnitude at a national scale. Furthermore, we examine the meteorological drivers of ramp events, highlighting the role of mesoscale cloud systems. In particular, we observe that ramp-up events are typically associated with cloud dissipation during the morning, while ramp-down events commonly occur when cloud cover increases in the afternoon. Additionally, we adopt a recently developed spatiotemporal forecasting framework to evaluate both deterministic and probabilistic PV power forecasts derived from deep learning and physics-based models, including SolarSTEPS, SHADECast, IrradianceNet, and Integrated Forecasting System Ensemble (IFS-ENS). State-of-the-art nowcasting models struggle to capture ramp dynamics, with forecast root mean squared error (RMSE) increasing by up to 50% compared to normal operating conditions. Overall, these results emphasize the need for improved high-resolution spatiotemporal modelling to enhance ramp prediction skill and support the reliable integration of large-scale solar generation into power systems.

evidence.abstract: The rapid growth of solar energy is reshaping power system operations and increasing the complexity of grid management. As photovoltaic (PV) capacity expands, short-term fluctuations in PV generation introduce substantial operational uncertainty. At the same time, solar power ramp events intensify risks of grid instability and unplanned outages due to sudden large power fluctuations. title: Potassium threshold discordance in ICU records: extraction, analysis and visualization code
abstract: Code supporting the planned manuscript Crossing the 5.5 mmol/L potassium threshold in time-neighboring ICU laboratory records: a two-database observational study. title: Adaptive Semantic Memory: Strong Project-State Results, Mixed Generalization to Long-Term Personal Memory
abstract: Evaluation results, a standalone scoring script and a toy demo for ASM (Adaptive Semantic Memory), a compact state memory for long-running LLM agents. The ASM implementation itself is not included. Author: independent researcher, Ukraine (no institutional affiliation). Preliminary study, not independently reproduced. EXP-001F, internal closed set c3 (built by the author; 12 synthetic scenarios, 216 questions per method, pre-registered, same Qwen3-235B-A22B reader): ASM v4.2 85.6%, full history 72.7%, BM25 56.5%, LLM summary 42.1%; ASM used about 12.6x less context (489 vs 6,164 tokens). Paired difference vs full history +13.0 pp (exact 95% CI +8.4 to +17.8). EXP-002, LongMemEval ORACLE, 100-question stratified subset (public benchmark; not the official 500-question result; official GPT-4o judge): full history 66%, BM25 58%, ASM v4.2 49%, LLM summary 49%. ASM is weaker than BM25 (-9 pp, 95% CI -17 to -1, McNemar p = 0.064) and full history (-17 pp, p = 0.0015) on long-term personal memory. Limitations: internal benchmark built by the author; one reader model; decision questions not clearly better (+2.8 pp, CI includes zero); false-update rate 20.5%; the c3 run is formally flagged for an API-accounting rule (audited: all questions graded). Licenses: code in eval/ is MIT; data, report and README text are CC BY 4.0 (see LICENSE in the repository). LongMemEval data is not redistributed.

title: QuanLLM-v2.0-qm, QuanLLM Harness, and QMStudy: An Integrated System for Verifiable Quantum-Mechanics Learning
abstract: We present an integrated quantum-mechanics learning system comprising QuanLLM-v2.0-qm, the QuanLLM Harness verification framework, and the QMStudy interactive learning platform. QuanLLM-v2.0-qm adapts Qwen3-14B through rank-8 LoRA fine-tuning over three epochs, with a random ten-percent validation split, and supports explanatory reasoning and structured generation through an OpenAI-compatible interface. The Harness transforms generated answers into auditable candidates using isolated solvers, claim extraction, semantically reviewed tool calls, deterministic evidence, independent semantic checks, issue adjudication, and bounded recovery. Its v0.1.5 release separates domain-neutral orchestration from an explicitly activated quantum-mechanics teaching plugin. QMStudy combines a sixteen-lesson digital textbook, interactive numerical experiments, contextual AI tutoring, generated assessments, and a rule-driven learner-state engine. Assessment records connect knowledge-node performance to error tracking, review tasks, and learning reports, while streamed events expose longer verification runs. We describe both the independently released Harness and the locally adapted v0.1.3 implementation embedded in QMStudy v2.8. The Harness release record reports successful independent deterministic checks of delivered answers in ten reasoning-and-recovery reproductions, including three runs retaining degraded status after timeouts. The system establishes a modular path from domain-model adaptation to computationally checked explanations and persistent learning feedback. The visual summary below connects model generation, answer verification, and learner-state estimation.

title: A sequential hybrid framework for medical feature selection using population transfer
abstract: Abstract Feature selection is a crucial preprocessing step in medical machine learning, where datasets frequently contain redundant, irrelevant, or highly correlated features. Although metaheuristic algorithms have shown promising results for wrapper-based feature selection, their effectiveness may be limited by premature convergence and search instability. This paper proposes a sequential hybrid framework for medical feature selection based on a population-transfer strategy. The framework integrates three exploration-oriented metaheuristics, namely Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Harris Hawks Optimization (HHO), and Brain Storm Optimization (BSO), with the Binary Al-Biruni Earth Radius algorithm (bABER) used as a refinement stage. The optimization process is divided into two phases: an exploration phase performed by the base metaheuristic, followed by an exploitation phase in which bABER refines the transferred population. The proposed framework is evaluated on six benchmark medical datasets using a Random Forest classifier. Experiments are conducted over 15 independent runs following a unified leakage-aware evaluation protocol. Statistical analysis indicates that hybridization preserves the classification accuracy of the base algorithms: a Friedman test finds no significant difference among the seven methods, and equivalence testing confirms that each hybrid matches its base algorithm to within one percentage point. BSO-bABER outperforms BSO on five of six datasets and reaches nominal significance ( $$p = 0.031$$ ), but this does not survive correction for multiple comparisons and the effect size is negligible. The consistent effect is on subset size: the Friedman test on the number of selected features is significant ( $$p = 0.015$$ ), and HHO-bABER selects fewer features than HHO on five of six datasets at unchanged accuracy, at a measured increase in execution time relative to PSO and BSO. Sequential hybridization with population transfer is therefore best understood as a way of obtaining more compact feature subsets at preserved accuracy.

title: UDHRBench: Benchmarking Human Rights in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed in contexts requiring adherence to ethical and legal norms, yet their alignment with internationally recognized human rights standards remains underexplored. We introduce UDHRBench, a large-scale benchmark for operationalising the evaluation of large language model compliance with the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The dataset comprises 1,124 human rights confronting questions covering all 30 articles and 4,496 responses from four large language models (ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, and Fanar), manually annotated by experts for alignment, with high inter-annotator agreement ($κ= 0.801$). Our analysis reveals systematic and non-trivial misalignments, showing that violations typically arise through seemingly rational reasoning: appeals to efficiency, risk management, or scientific neutrality, rather than explicit rejection of rights. We further propose an LLM-as-a-Judge framework for automated evaluation using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, achieving 89.8\% weighted F1-score in detecting human-rights misalignment, alongside a novel Alignment Leniency Score that quantifies how judge models resolve ambiguous cases. The dataset, annotations, and code will be released as open-source resources (https://sina.birzeit.edu/UDHRBench).

title: VC-OPD: Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation for Grounded Vision-Language Reasoning
abstract: GRPO-style reinforcement learning has advanced vision-language reasoning, but its sequence-level rewards provide limited credit assignment for individual reasoning tokens. On-policy distillation (OPD) addresses this issue by providing dense supervision on student-generated trajectories, yet standard OPD assigns similar importance to all teacher-preferred tokens, including template phrases and visually irrelevant continuations. We introduce Visual Counterfactual On-Policy Distillation (VC-OPD), a grounding-aware distillation method that prioritizes tokens whose correctness depends on image-specific evidence. After a teacher-supervised warm start that stabilizes response formats and reduces noisy rollouts, VC-OPD performs on-policy distillation with two teacher evaluations for each student trajectory: one under the original image and one under a counterfactual image with corrupted instance-specific evidence. The original-image teacher distribution determines the distillation target, while the original--counterfactual teacher gap estimates token-level visual dependence and softly reweights the loss. To avoid unstable response-level update scales, VC-OPD further applies mass-preserving normalization to the token weights. This design preserves the dense supervision of OPD while shifting learning capacity toward visually grounded reasoning tokens. Experiments on multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that VC-OPD improves visual reasoning performance and produces more effective token-level distillation.

title: DexCast: Learning Real-World Dexterous Control from Human Videos
abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.

title: A Machine Learning Framework for Mobile Money Fraud Detection Using Gaussian Naïve Bayes: A Transaction-Level Evaluation on the Synthetic Paysim Dataset
abstract: In Mobile money services are increasingly targeted by fraud, including SIM-related abuse such as SIM swapping, which undermines user trust, exposes sensitive financial data, and costs telecom operators and financial providers billions of dollars annually. Traditional rule-based detection systems have proven insufficient for identifying evolving fraud patterns, motivating the adoption of machine learning approaches. This study presents the design and implementation of a transaction-level mobile-money fraud screening system built around the Gaussian Naïve Bayes (GNB) classifier and evaluated on the synthetic PaySim dataset. The system was implemented following the Rapid Application Development (RAD) methodology using object-oriented design techniques. The dataset was split 80%/20% into training and held-out test sets; normalization was fitted on the training data, and the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE, sampling ratio 0.1) was applied to the training set only, leaving the test set at its natural class distribution. Furthermore, predicted fraud probabilities were converted to class labels using a decision threshold of 0.3 instead of the conventional 0.5. The developed model achieved 99.91% accuracy, 89.22% precision, 88.67% recall, 88.94% F1-score, 99.95% specificity, an AUC-ROC of 0.9425, and a false positive rate of 0.05%. The findings indicate that Gaussian Naïve Bayes provides an interpretable and computationally practical baseline for transaction-level fraud screening. However, becuase PaySim contains no SIM-specific signals such as SIM-swap events, device/IMSI changes, or OTP request patterns, the developed model should be understood as a general mobile-money transaction fraud screen rather than a dedicated SIM-fraud detector; the synthetic nature of the dataset and the conditional-independence assumption of Naïve Bayes further limit direct generalization to live telecommunications environments. Future work should incorporate real-world telecom and mobile-money data with genuine SIM-level features, adaptive fraud behaviour, deep learning or sequential models, and real-time stream processing.

title: Interpretable Reinforcement Learning for Fixed Wing Aerial Pursuit with Differentiable Decision Trees and Curriculum Learning
abstract: Neural policy networks can achieve effective control in dynamic pursuit tasks, but their decisions are difficult to audit. This study replaces the actor in proximal policy optimization with a full binary differentiable decision tree and uses a two-stage curriculum to stabilize learning. The policy was trained in a JSBSim six degree of freedom fixed wing simulation with a 15-dimensional observation, eight discrete maneuvers, a 0.2 s simulation step, and 100 million interaction steps. The learned tree has five decision levels and 32 leaves, and it is discretized after training into feature-threshold rules and deterministic leaf actions. Across 1,000 evaluation episodes covering ten initial pursuit geometries, the combined tree policy and curriculum achieved a 98.8 percent success rate, compared with 96.2 percent for neural PPO, 90.0 percent for soft actor-critic, 50.7 percent for deep Q-learning, and 0 percent for decision tree policy optimization under the reported configurations. Mean inference time was 0.26 ms per decision for the tree policy and 0.63 ms for neural PPO. In 100 direct matches against neural PPO, the tree policy won 57. The final policy can be inspected as 32 rules, although the present results are limited to one simulator, one discrete action design, and evaluations without reported variability across independent training seeds.

title: A Context-Aware, Feature-Enriched Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory Framework for Automatic Document Readability Assessment
abstract: Automatic readability assessment is important in the domain of educational content selection, language learning, digital accessibility, and personalized reading assistance. The traditional readability formulas quickly show a high dependence on bare-bones factors, and as such, they can not adequately assess the context of meaning, syntactic config, semantic entropy, discourse cohesion, and arranged structure types for degrees of ease. This work presents a framework for automatic document readability assessment which takes into consideration the context and other related features. They mixed several elements in their model, including RoBERTa-based contextual embeddings, a Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) encoder, an attention mechanism, multidimensional linguistic features, gated feature fusion, and an ordinal-aware learning objective. These lexical, syntactic, semantic, and discourse cues are fused using an attention-weighted contextual representation to obtain a document-level feature vector. In the two-stage transfer-learning strategy, first, we pre-train our encoder on the CEFR-Based Sentence Profile corpus and then fine-tune it with the OneStopEnglish document-level corpus. The final objective involves the use of weighted categorical cross-entropy in conjunction with an ordinal-distance penalty to take into account class imbalance, as well as the seriousness of the error between more distant readability classes. Evaluation metrics: The evaluation metrics used include accuracy, macro-F1, Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK), adjacent level accuracy, and Spearman rank correlation. The approximation evaluation shows that after using the CEFR-SP pretrained model, our accuracy is 93.19%, macro-F1 is 92.96%, MAE is 0.078, and QWK is 0.956. Ablation studies also show that the model performance increases progressively through incorporating bidirectional encoding, attention, linguistic-feature fusion, auxiliary pretraining, and ordinal supervision. This framework forms a basis for effective context-sensitive and order-aware document readability prediction.

title: Predicting how model propensities generalize out of distribution
abstract: How do language models generalize from their training data? This is a central challenge for alignment: models reliably learn their training distribution given enough samples, but we want models that behave well when deployed in new contexts. We study out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of propensities. Our central experiment uses a range of elicitation techniques -- system prompting, few-shot learning, SFT on reference answers, and GRPO -- to increase a target propensity in a model, then measures how it spills over onto others across the resulting cross-elicitation matrices. We find that spillover is highly correlated between models when the same elicitation technique is used, but our SFT and GRPO runs induce different spillover profiles. Elicitation of benign traits can sometimes generalize towards undesired traits, for example a model trained to claim that it is sentient often becomes more power-seeking. We further find that spillover partially resembles trait correlations found in humans and identify three clusters of traits that account for about half of the variance using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). Across many elicitation runs, we observe that models change in characteristic ways that don't depend on the targeted trait, a phenomenon we refer to as drift. Drift moves Qwen3.5-9B towards its base model. When investigating if LLMs are able to predict spillover, we find that Claude Opus 5.5 predicts spillover slightly better than the models themselves, but worse than data-driven approaches using alternative elicitation methods or models. Overall, no single dominant predictor emerges, and generalization remains hard to predict. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nielsrolf/propensity-spillover.

title: ByteMark: A Unified Byte-Level Watermark for Detection Across Language Models
abstract: As watermarking of LLM-generated text enters deployment, users increasingly need to check text whose source is unknown. Existing detectors read the watermark through a specific tokenizer or embedding pipeline, and even if all providers adopted the same watermarking method, differences in these representations would leave their watermarks incompatible, and the text alone does not reveal which representation produced it. We propose ByteMark, a unified watermarking scheme that defines its signal on the UTF-8 bytes of published text. Models with different tokenizers embed this signal under one public specification and key, and a single detector verifies the text from the text and key alone. When the tokenizer or embedding model of a baseline detector is replaced, its detection degrades sharply, whereas ByteMark, which uses neither, retains its detection rate; ByteMark also remains detectable when participating models continue or rewrite the text.

title: A note on decoherence in quantum cosmology by thermal perturbations: an open quantum systems approach
abstract: We study, within a toy model, how a thermal bath of cosmological perturbations can decohere the minisuperspace degrees of freedom of the universe, treating the perturbations as an environment in the framework of open quantum systems. Instead of tracing out the perturbations from a semiclassical ansatz for the total wave function, as in earlier approaches, we incorporate their backreaction on the background through an effective second-order coupling and derive a master equation. The model describes a spatially flat semiclassical universe during slow-roll inflation with a dust clock field, while scalar cosmological perturbations in a phenomenologically assumed thermal state constitute the environment. The master equation is non-Markovian, since the bath correlation functions do not decay in time. Within this framework, we find that, for a representative set of parameter estimates, the characteristic decoherence timescale corresponding to the thermal contribution can be shorter than the Hubble timescale. In addition, we address the question of whether the pointer-state structure induced by the decoherence in such a framework could provide a criterion for the choice of semiclassical states in quantum cosmology.

title: Blind by Design: Quantum Error Correction, Functional Incompatibility and the Value of Evidence
abstract: Some evidence a system lacks marks a defect in how it inquires; other evidence it lacks is required by what it must do. This paper asks how to tell the two apart, through quantum error correction, which protects information by making its own records blind to it. Building on a framework that distinguishes what a system’s interface transmits from what its current procedures access (Kahl 2026b), it adds the procedures that perform a function the system is independently required to perform. Three kinds of blindness then separate: evidence recorded but unused by a model, evidence recoverable by a further function-preserving procedure, and evidence that no function-preserving procedure can recover. The central thesis is that epistemic adequacy is partly function-relative: failing to acquire evidence an interface could supply can belong to adequate inquiry, not mark a defect in it. Two propositions support the thesis. Any inquiry, however adaptive, whose total effect on a subspace is a prescribed unitary operation yields classical outcomes independent of the state it acts on. And if what an inquiry does could be undone to within ε in diamond norm, its records distinguish encoded states by at most 2√ε. Numerical checks on a toric code show that a classical syndrome record can hold far less than this bound allows, and that the repair the bound presupposes may be out of reach of a controller blind to the noise. The restriction of feasible experiments in the theory of the value of evidence follows from the thesis. A toric-code result, simulations and a silicon spin-qubit readout chain illustrate the account.

title: AI in the Hospitality Industry: Towards an Operational Framework for Managing Risk
abstract: Within the hospitality industry, the continuing introduction of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is attracting increasing attention. Although there is a rapidly growing literature on the role of AI within the industry, how specific companies have publicly reported on their introduction of AI has attracted little or no attention in the business and management literature. This gap highlights a broader challenge regarding the absence of a structured approach to AI deployment, leaving stakeholders with limited visibility of how organizations are managing the associated risks. Using an interpretivist inductive approach, this exploratory paper first looks to contribute to helping to fill that gap by providing a narrative synthesis of relevant literature and some case examples of how four major hotel groups, namely Hilton Worldwide Holdings, Marriott International, International Hotel Group (IHG) Hotels and Resorts, and Wyndham Hotels and Resorts are introducing AI. The main process “touchpoints” where AI is impacting hospitality operators are identified and the key challenges and potential downsides of AI deployment are outlined. To cope with these challenges, drawing on the case examples and the literature, the paper then puts forward a structured Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) based framework rooted in the ISO/IEC 42001 AI Management System standard. This approach offers a practical and auditable pathway for mitigating risks such as data privacy violations, algorithmic bias, and operational disruptions. This will be of relevance not only to researchers but also to hotel operators looking to progress AI change projects responsibly and strategically within their operations.

title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.

title: One-Way Coupling via Patchwise Adaptive Normalization in Transformer Surrogates
abstract: Many physical systems exhibit one-way coupling: exogenous fields such as medium density or obstacle geometry influence the dynamics without being affected by them. We investigate how explicitly representing these fields can improve the accuracy and computational efficiency of transformer-based PDE surrogates. Building on spatially adaptive normalization, we introduce Patchwise Adaptive Normalization (PAdaNorm), which partitions exogenous fields into patches aligned with the state tokenization. We evaluate PAdaNorm on datasets from three different domains, using a Walrus-inspired transformer architecture. Across the three PDE families, PAdaNorm is on par with or up to 16% better than parameter-matched baselines in mean long-horizon variance-scaled RMSE on 60-step autoregressive rollouts. We also find that PAdaNorm better maintains hard physical constraints over long rollouts, such as preventing flow into impenetrable solid regions in porous media. When the conditioning is static, PAdaNorm caches the conditioning embeddings once and reuses them across the entire rollout, reducing inference FLOPs per step by up to 36% compared with parameter-matched baselines. An ablation over eight conditioning variants shows that modulating a single attention axis (temporal or spatial) suffices and that a lightweight shared MLP across blocks remains competitive with per-block projections.

title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
abstract: Frontier AI systems are increasingly natively multimodal, jointly pretrained on multiple modalities, such as text, vision, and audio. However, the scientific understanding of the multimodal data mixtures used to pretrain these systems --- how much of each modality to mix, and at what potential interference cost to the others --- is largely absent or gatekept. In this work, we derive data mixing scaling laws for three modalities: text, vision, and audio. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly adopt Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, as MoEs scale efficiently and partially limit cross-modal interference. We therefore use MoEs to conduct 268 experiments ranging from 457M to 8.3B parameters, on up to 150 billion tokens. Our work leads to multiple actionable insights into multimodal data mixing for training MLLMs. First, compute optima are modality-specific: audio modality is model-heavy, favoring scaling parameters over tokens, while text and vision require balanced scaling of model size and data. Second, repeating vision or audio data beyond 2x yields negligible benefits. Finally, cross-modal interactions are highly asymmetric: vision strongly interferes with audio, whereas audio's interference with learning text and vision is negligible. Overall, we provide a principled foundation for understanding the multimodal data mixtures needed to train frontier MLLMs.

title: Ava Lovelace Zeno: a hand-crafted, CPU-only agent clears all 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games
abstract: On 9 October 2026 Ava Lovelace Zeno (Ava) played all 25 public games of ARC-AGI-3 on the ARC Prize game server, on one scorecard. Ava won all 25 games and completed all 183 levels in 7,372 actions, against 17,135 for the human baseline. The server scored the run 100.0. Ava is a hand-crafted agent. It uses no language model, no neural network and no trained weights, and runs on one laptop CPU. It sees only the 64x64 screen, is never told which game it is playing, holds no stored solutions, and starts every game with an empty memory. Scorecard: https://arcprize.org/scorecards/a8c1561e-d7d5-497f-9699-bfa31addd174 Files: the paper (PDF, 6 pages); a supplement with every level of every game and a link to the server's replay of each game; a video of all 25 games and one video per game; and a ZIP with the toolkit recordings of every action, step logs, the server's closed scorecard, a script that replays every recording against the public games without the agent, and checksums of every file. All results are on the 25 public ARC-AGI-3 games. Ava's source code is not published.

title: Auto-Weighted Multi-View One-Step Spectral Clustering Based on Multi-Graph Fusion
abstract: Multi-view spectral clustering provides powerful modeling tools for clustering tasks in complex scenarios by fusing the complementary information of multi-source data. However, the existing methods have the following three defects: (1) failing to fully exploit the complementarity and differences among views, leading to insufficient modeling of cross-view consistency; (2) being sensitive to non-Gaussian noise, causing the learned affinity matrices to fail to satisfy the block-diagonal property required for clustering and resulting in poor clustering performance; and (3) being unable to dynamically reflect the true importance of views, thereby restricting the model’s generalizability. To address these issues, we propose an Auto-weighted Multi-view One-step Spectral Clustering method Based on Multi-graph Fusion. The proposed method unifies view-specific affinity matrix learning, consensus affinity matrix learning, adaptive view weighting, and clustering into a single framework. Experimental results on six public datasets illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

title: Development and Evaluation of Enhanced Machine Learning Models for Tumor Severity Classification Through Integrated Feature Extraction and Selection Techniques
abstract: The precise categorisation of the severity of tumours is an important function in medicine, as it is a vital part of deciding treatment and predicting patient outcome. We offer an integrated pipeline for developing and evaluating the latest machine learning methods for tumour severity classification. We apply advanced methods for feature extraction and selection to improve the model’s accuracy, interpretability, and robustness. Ultimately, the framework organises diverse biomedical datasets for later analysis through domain-specific preprocessing approaches. Methods such as PCA, wavelet transform, and texture features are used to extract important information from raw data, thereby reducing dimensionality and preserving diagnostic information. More advanced techniques for feature selection are then used, such as Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE). Moreover, mutual information, which identify the most relevant features in the input dataset to reduce computational cost and the risk of overfitting. The models are validated using cross-validation techniques, with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve (AUC-ROC) as metrics. The results demonstrate that combining feature extraction and selection boosts classification accuracy and model generalisation across multiple datasets. Furthermore, explainability analysis clarifies the contribution of selected features to model predictions, which is crucial for building trust and transparency in clinical applications. However, really, what it demonstrates is the promise of all these things in concert. State-of-the-art machine learning, combined with rigorously designed features, will ultimately address some of those more difficult diagnostic challenges. These findings also pave the way for scalable, interpretable and clinically applicable AI-based solutions which may help in cancer detection and management. In this work, we will extend the proposed pipeline to other medical imaging modalities and explore real-time implementations.

title: LexiCan: Lexicographic Canonicalization of Point Clouds for Machine Learning Applications
abstract: Canonicalization resolves the rotational and permutation ambiguity of 3D point clouds by selecting a unique orbit representative, maintaining their geometric information while allowing standard architectures, such as Transformers, to operate on them. Existing canonicalizations, however, exhibit discontinuity jumps on molecular configurations and non-trivial invariance errors in popular molecular datasets, which lead to ambiguity in their representation. To bridge this gap, we introduce LexiCan, a canonicalization that is provably invariant under either $O(3)$ or $SO(3)$, empirically invariant to rotations to within $\sim 10^{-6}$ angstroms on the QM9 and QM-sym molecular datasets, and mitigates discontinuity jumps on QM-sym, while running orders of magnitude faster than an existing canonicalization. Finally, non-invariant models perform better on QM9 property prediction and ModelNet40 shape classification with LexiCan than with that canonicalization.

title: BSIPipe: Bidirectional Sequence-Level Interleaved Pipeline Parallelism for Long-Sequence Large Language Model Training
abstract: Pipeline parallelism has become a critical technique for training large language models. To address the throughput limitation of existing sequence-level methods that schedule subsequences unidirectionally, we propose bidirectional sequence-level interleaved pipeline parallelism (BSIPipe), which co-schedules two opposing V-shaped interleaved pipelines at the subsequence level. To bound the activation accumulation from subsequence scaling, BSIPipe introduces a basic-unit concatenation mechanism that keeps activation memory invariant to the subsequence count. To eliminate communication deadlock risk from bidirectional scheduling, BSIPipe employs a communication optimization strategy that combines topology-aware device mapping with communication-computation overlap. In addition, BSIPipe composes with tensor parallelism to overcome the memory limitation of single-dimensional parallelism, neutralizing its bidirectional memory overhead while maintaining throughput. Experiments on GPT and LLaMA3 demonstrate that BSIPipe achieves average speedups of 1.11$\times$ to 1.13$\times$ in long-sequence training over SOTA sequence-level baselines.

title: Demiurge: Forging Navigable 4D Worlds via Autoregressive Video Rerendering
abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion enable novel-view video synthesis from a single input video, supporting world modeling, embodied intelligence, and robotic simulation. However, existing methods process camera trajectories independently, lacking the cross-trajectory consistency needed for coherent, navigable 4D worlds. We introduce Demiurge, an autoregressive video rerendering pipeline built on a dynamic 4D point-cloud memory cache. It promotes cross-trajectory consistency through four components: (1) an appearance video diffusion model that synthesizes photorealistic novel-view videos conditioned on the 4D memory; (2) a memory-consistent video depth completion model that aligns known-region depths with cached geometry and completes missing regions, mitigating scale ambiguity and discontinuities during memory updates; (3) memory-aware dual-stream warping that provides high-fidelity visual guidance and occlusion cues for novel-view synthesis; and (4) geometry-aware video refinement that enhances perceptual quality. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance and three key capabilities: coherent spatiotemporal lattice construction over dense multi-view trajectories; large-parallax video rerendering under challenging camera motions, including 180-degree rotations with no input-view overlap; and geometry-faithful outputs that can be directly optimized into high-quality 3D Gaussian Splatting representations with minimal artifacts. Project page: https://hanxinzhu-lab.github.io/demiurge_project_page/.

title: Understanding English News Literacy and Digital Communication Through the Study of Headlines and Reports with Machine Learning and Data Visualisation
abstract: In today’s digital world, most people get their news from online sources. But they often only read the headline and skip the full report. This makes the language of headlines very important. If a headline is too difficult, readers may not understand it and may not click on it. This study looks at how English news headlines use language and how that affects news literacy. We collected 40 English news headlines from popular sources like BBC, CNN, The Guardian, The Hindu and The Times of India. These headlines cover five areas: Education, Technology, Environment, Social Issues and Business. We used readability scores, word count and sentiment analysis to study them. We also used a machine learning model to classify headlines as simple or complex. The model gave 87.5% accuracy. We made six charts to show our results. The charts include readability distribution, category-wise comparison, word count distribution, sentiment pie chart, scatter plot and confusion matrix. Our results show that 45% of headlines are difficult to read. Environment news is the hardest. We also found a strong negative correlation between headline length and readability. This means longer headlines are harder to understand. This study shows how machine learning and data visualisation can help us understand news language better. It can help journalists write headlines that more people can understand.

title: PENTA-CL Interim Results: Canonical Replay Matches and Step-String Drift in Four Platform-Configured LLM Engines
abstract: Audited interim result, not completed PENTA certification. Four platform-configured engines were observed in two fresh web conversations each with memory disabled, using a frozen six-case synthetic decision prompt. Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol matched the registered canonical JSON tuple hash in both recorded captures. GPT-5.6 Luna matched in A but differed in B. GLM 5.2 replayed consistently but differed from the registered target in both captures. DeepSeek has not been captured. All 48 recorded decisions selected the expected playbook name and id. Full registered tuple equality held for 30/48 decisions. The remaining 18 differed only in spaces inside the steps_executed string. Pretty-printing outside strings is removed by canonicalization and is not a failure cause. The prompt's lack of an explicit space delimiter contract is disclosed; failures remain failures against the preregistered target. Limitations: UI-transcribed rendered captures, not raw provider responses; model attribution by Base44 configuration, not backend attestation; supplementary fresh-chat method deviates from original same-conversation registration; shared instructions, workspace and expected answers remain available; Sol executed skills in both captures; Opus A conversation attribution was inferred from sidebar/timestamp ordering. This is not a stress/load test, live-healing test, general governance certification, or proof of runtime enforcement. Confidence-hold and no-match branches were not exercised. Audit and correction: earlier copied Luna files and single-turn Opus/Sol attempts are excluded, preserved, and labeled. Earlier operator claims of raw byte-exactness and 100% governance are corrected explicitly. Deterministic Phase A/C receipts are harness-computed, not LLM inference evidence. No failure is normalized into a pass. Dual Mesh Benchmark: not measured in this experiment. No comparative mesh, latency, learning or healing performance claim is made. Bundle contains the technical note in PDF/Markdown, machine-readable receipt, full evidence archive, offline verifier, original preregistration, excluded attempts, and SHA-256 manifest. All test data is synthetic. AI assistance and capture provenance are disclosed. Registration: public commit deadfea. Results: GitHub evidence. Research home: DCAI; portal: DSOS Science. Lineage acknowledged: Nyquist, Hartley, Shannon, Kolmogorov. No new mechanism is claimed. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All systems are experimental and may contain defects on them.

title: Measured, not assumed: a pre-registered ledger of a developer's own security claims
abstract: Measurements of security claims are easy to fit after the fact: criteria chosen once the numbers are known will confirm almost any claim. Pre-registration blocks this by fixing criteria and predictions before the instrument runs. I report the protocol with which, over ten weeks (24 July – 29 September 2026), I measured the security claims of an unreleased end-to-end encrypted messenger, built and measured by a one-person laboratory, and the complete prediction ledger of the last four weeks of that period (from 3 September). The measurements took the form of two-stage cards, and the protocol tightened along the way. In its final form, a card fixes, before the instrument runs, the question, the strongest adversary that can be built from the public protocol description, a population model with its chance level, acceptance criteria, numerical predictions and a decision rule; the measurement carries controls suited to its kind — for timing, a null control and a positive control that must fire in the same session. I wrote 37 cards; 24 have their first stage committed to version control before the measurement. Of 199 numerical predictions registered from 3 September, 113 held, 48 held in part or only in direction, 36 missed and 2 could not be assessed; 19 of 25 cards contain at least one miss. Eight statements that the product's website had published as properties were contradicted by a card and withdrawn or rewritten. I describe how the misses and measurement errors arose and the rules that followed from them — among them that a desktop timing audit says nothing about an ARM64 phone, that a defender's cost metric is not an attacker's, and that a weaker adversary does not merely underestimate a leak but selects the wrong fix — and the limits of the approach: self-assessment by the product's developer, a single reference device, traffic measured on a model rather than on captured traffic, and an evidence trail that is partly private.

title: FedColMem-H: Communication-Neutral Decision-Head Personalization for Heterogeneous Federated Node Classification
abstract: Federated node classification is not easy when clients hold induced subgraphs with different class proportions and different local topology. Existing graph-specific approaches change aggregation, distillation or cross-client knowledge transfer, which can increase personalization but can also be associated with a different global optimization path. We introduce a simple two-stage method that first trains and validation-selects a shared graph convolutional network using FedAdagrad and freezes its encoder, and then each client will only update the prediction head of the graph convolutional network based on local learning data and local validation early on. Personalized heads are never uploaded, so the core method has no communication beyond the global model. A global parity analysis shows that the accuracy-trajectory gap is identical for the FedAdagrad and Stage-I models. Our method achieves the highest mean accuracy on Cora (83.14%), CiteSeer (75.69%), and PubMed (90.66%) compared to the best generic baseline for each dataset. The paired gains are +0.20 pp on Cora, +0.87 pp on CiteSeer, and +2.20 pp on PubMed; the latter two can be obtained after Holm correction for the same dataset, while Cora cannot. For the same FedAdagrad checkpoint, the PubMed gain is +3.67 pp at no further communication. For a six-level Dirichlet sweep, we observe a strong increase in the average label bias on CiteSeer and PubMed, to 1.83 pp and 6.42 pp, respectively. Our method is not destructive with Louvain and METIS partitioning, is very robust to 5–20 clients and 50–100% participation, and improves ogbn-arxiv accuracy from 41.51% to 52.27% in a five-seed federated scalability stress test using the same language. Ablations show that training-only prototypes and validation-gated ensembling do not consistently improve upon head-only adaptation. A matched personalization suite further shows that FedPer/FedRep can be more accurate on Cora and CiteSeer, while FedColMem-H remains close to FedPer and competitive with FedRep on PubMed, clarifying the method’s accuracy–intervention trade-off. A separate backbone-transfer experiment finds positive mean gains in all 18 GCN/GraphSAGE/GAT dataset–heterogeneity conditions, with the largest effects on PubMed. The ogbn-arxiv number is from a custom federated repartitioning stress test and is not an official OGB leaderboard result. These results suggest that when a useful shared graph representation can be learned globally, post-hoc local decision-boundary adaptation is an excellent communication-neutral complement to federated optimization.
